title: What are the first five books of the Bible collectively called?
answer: The Pentateuch, or the Torah ("instruction"); Jews also call it "the Law of Moses."
note: Torah means instruction rather than legislation, which is why narrative occupies more of the Pentateuch than law. Jesus' phrase 'the law of Moses, and the prophets, and the psalms' (Luke 24:44) reflects the threefold Hebrew canon still in use.

title: With what four words does the Bible open?
answer: "In the beginning God" — Scripture assumes God rather than arguing for him.
note: The verse simultaneously denies atheism, polytheism, pantheism, and materialism in one clause.

title: On which day of creation were the sun, moon and stars made?
answer: The fourth day — after light itself on day one.
note: Light on day one and luminaries on day four is not a scientific oversight but a polemical structure: Israel's neighbours worshipped sun and moon, and Genesis demotes them to lamps installed on day four, not even named directly.

title: What did God declare about creation on the sixth day?
answer: That it was "very good" — the only day given that superlative.
note: 'Very good' is a moral and aesthetic verdict on the whole, not a claim of perfection in the sense of completion — the mandate to subdue and cultivate assumes work still to be done.

title: What does it mean that humanity is made in the "image of God"?
answer: Every person bears God's likeness in reason, moral will, relationship and rule over creation — the ground of all human dignity.
note: Cited in Gen 9:6 as the reason murder is capital, and in Jas 3:9 against cursing people.

title: What two trees stood in the middle of Eden?
answer: The tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
note: The prohibition concerned only one tree; the tree of life was freely available until after the fall. The exile from Eden is therefore an act of mercy as well as judgment, preventing endless life in a fallen state.

title: What was the first thing God called "not good"?
answer: That the man should be alone.

title: What is the first promise of a Redeemer in Scripture called?
answer: The protoevangelium — the seed of the woman bruising the serpent's head.

title: What sign sealed the Noahic covenant?
answer: The rainbow, God's pledge never again to destroy the earth by flood.

title: What three promises formed God's call to Abram?
answer: A great nation, a great name and personal blessing, and blessing to all families of the earth through him.
note: Paul calls the third clause "the gospel preached beforehand unto Abraham" (Gal 3:8).

title: Which verse is the Old Testament foundation for justification by faith?
answer: "He believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness."
note: Quoted by Paul in Rom 4:3 and Gal 3:6, and by James in Jas 2:23.

title: What was the sign of the Abrahamic covenant?
answer: Circumcision of every male on the eighth day.
note: Circumcision marks the organ of generation, tying the covenant sign to the promise of seed; Paul's argument in Romans 4:10-11 turns on the fact that Abraham was justified before receiving it.

title: What name did God give Moses at the burning bush?
answer: "I AM THAT I AM" — the self-existent, eternal One.
note: The Hebrew 'ehyeh asher ehyeh' can be rendered 'I will be what I will be,' suggesting God's self-definition is disclosed in action over time — which is why the exodus itself becomes the name's commentary.

title: How many plagues struck Egypt, and what was the last?
answer: Ten; the last was the death of the firstborn.
note: Each plague targets a specific Egyptian deity — the Nile, the sun, cattle — so the sequence is a systematic demonstration that Egypt's gods cannot protect their own domains.

title: What protected Israel's firstborn on Passover night?
answer: The blood of a lamb without blemish, struck on the lintel and doorposts.
note: Paul: "our passover also hath been sacrificed, even Christ" (1 Cor 5:7).

title: How did God lead Israel through the wilderness?
answer: By a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night.
note: The pillar of cloud and fire is the first sustained image of divine guidance in Scripture, and its unpredictability — moving or resting without notice — is the point of Numbers 9:15-23.

title: What food did God provide daily in the wilderness, and what does the name mean?
answer: Manna — from the question "What is it?"

title: On which mountain was the Law given?
answer: Mount Sinai (also called Horeb).
note: Sinai's terror in Exodus 19-20 is deliberately contrasted with Zion in Hebrews 12:18-24: the readers have come not to a mountain that might be touched and burned with fire, but to the city of the living God.

title: What is the first commandment of the Decalogue?
answer: "Thou shalt have none other gods before me."
note: The prologue — 'I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt' — precedes every command, so obedience is framed as a response to redemption already accomplished.

title: Which commandment carries a promise attached?
answer: Honour thy father and thy mother — "that thy days may be long."
note: Paul notes in Ephesians 6:2 that it is 'the first commandment with promise,' and the promise of long life in the land ties family stability to national survival.

title: What did Israel make while Moses was on the mountain?
answer: A golden calf, fashioned by Aaron from their earrings.

title: What was the Ark of the Covenant, and what did it contain?
answer: The gold-covered chest in the Holy of Holies, holding the tablets of the Law, Aaron's rod that budded, and a pot of manna.
note: The three contents — tablets, manna and Aaron's rod — memorialise three rebellions: against God's word, his provision and his appointed leadership. The mercy seat covered them all.

title: What sat on top of the Ark, and why did it matter?
answer: The mercy seat, between the cherubim — where God met Israel and where atoning blood was sprinkled.
note: Paul uses the same term of Christ, set forth as a propitiation (Rom 3:25).

title: What was the significance of the veil in the tabernacle?
answer: It barred access to the Holy of Holies, entered once a year by the high priest alone.
note: Torn top to bottom at Christ's death (Matt 27:51).

title: Who were the first priests of Israel?
answer: Aaron and his sons, of the tribe of Levi.
note: Aaron and his sons were consecrated over seven days (Lev 8), and the elaborate ordination underscores that no one takes this honour to himself — a point Hebrews 5:4 makes about Christ's priesthood.

title: What happened to Nadab and Abihu?
answer: They offered strange fire before the LORD and were consumed.

title: What is the central theme of Leviticus?
answer: Holiness — how a holy God may be approached and how a redeemed people must live.
note: 'Be ye holy; for I am holy' (Lev 11:44) is quoted directly in 1 Peter 1:16, transferring the whole book's logic to the church: holiness is derivative, grounded in God's character rather than in human achievement.

title: What five main offerings does Leviticus prescribe?
answer: Burnt, meal (grain), peace, sin, and trespass (guilt) offerings.

title: What happened on the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur)?
answer: The high priest entered the Holy of Holies with blood, and a scapegoat bore Israel's sins into the wilderness.
note: Hebrews 9-10 reads the whole ritual as a shadow of Christ's once-for-all offering.

title: Why was blood forbidden as food?
answer: "The life of the flesh is in the blood" — it was given for atonement upon the altar.
note: 'The life of the flesh is in the blood' (Lev 17:11) supplies the rationale for the entire sacrificial system — blood atones because it represents life given, not merely death inflicted.

title: What was the Year of Jubilee?
answer: Every fiftieth year: debts released, slaves freed, and ancestral land returned.
note: Jesus reads Isaiah's Jubilee language over his own ministry in Luke 4:18-19.

title: What is the sevenfold Levitical feast calendar?
answer: Passover, Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, Weeks (Pentecost), Trumpets, Atonement, and Tabernacles.

title: What is the Aaronic blessing?
answer: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee: the LORD make his face to shine upon thee..."
note: The threefold structure of Numbers 6:24-26 has been read since the Fathers as trinitarian in shape, and the silver amulets found at Ketef Hinnom bearing this text are the oldest known fragments of biblical writing.

title: Why did Israel wander forty years in the wilderness?
answer: For refusing to enter Canaan after the ten spies' evil report — a year for each day of spying.
note: Hebrews 3:19 gives the theological verdict: 'they could not enter in because of unbelief.' The wilderness generation becomes the New Testament's standing warning about hearing without faith.

title: Which two spies brought back a good report?
answer: Joshua and Caleb — the only men of that generation to enter the land.

title: What happened to Korah, Dathan and Abiram?
answer: The earth opened and swallowed them for rebelling against Moses' and Aaron's God-given authority.

title: What did Moses do that barred him from the promised land?
answer: He struck the rock at Meribah instead of speaking to it, failing to sanctify God before Israel.

title: What did Israel look at to be healed of serpent bites?
answer: The bronze serpent Moses lifted on a pole.
note: Jesus applies it directly to his crucifixion in John 3:14-15.

title: What is the Shema, and why is it central?
answer: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God is one LORD" — Israel's confession of monotheism and whole-hearted love for God.
note: Jesus names it the first and greatest commandment (Mark 12:29-30).

title: What test did Deuteronomy give for a true prophet?
answer: If the thing spoken does not come to pass, the LORD has not spoken it.

title: Which prophet "like unto Moses" did Deuteronomy promise?
answer: A future prophet whom God would raise up from among Israel's brethren.
note: Peter identifies him as Christ in Acts 3:22.

title: What two things did Moses set before Israel on the plains of Moab?
answer: Life and good, death and evil — blessing and cursing.

title: Where did Moses die, and who buried him?
answer: On Mount Nebo, in view of Canaan; the LORD buried him, and no man knows the place.

title: How old was Moses at his death, and what was his condition?
answer: 120 years — "his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated."

title: How does Deuteronomy summarise Moses' uniqueness?
answer: "There arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face."

title: What single command does Jesus join to the Shema as second?
answer: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself" — drawn from the Law itself.

title: What did God do on the seventh day, and what did he do to that day?
answer: He rested from his work, and he blessed and sanctified the seventh day.
note: The Sabbath is grounded in creation before it is grounded in Sinai, which is why Jesus can call it made 'for man' (Mark 2:27).

title: From what was the man formed, and what made him a living soul?
answer: From the dust of the ground; God breathed into his nostrils the breath of life.

title: What was the first recorded human sin's immediate effect on the couple?
answer: Their eyes were opened, they knew they were naked, and they hid from God.

title: Whose offering did God respect, Cain's or Abel's?
answer: Abel's — he brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof.

title: Who walked with God and 'was not, for God took him'?
answer: Enoch, the seventh from Adam.

title: What was the sin at Babel, and how did God judge it?
answer: Pride in building a tower to make a name; God confounded their language and scattered them.
note: Pentecost reverses Babel: tongues divide at Babel, tongues unite at Pentecost (Acts 2:6).

title: Who was Melchizedek, and what did he bring to Abram?
answer: King of Salem and priest of the Most High God; he brought forth bread and wine.
note: Hebrews 7 argues Christ's priesthood is of Melchizedek's order — royal, without recorded genealogy, and unending.

title: What did God change Abram's and Sarai's names to, and why?
answer: Abraham ('father of a multitude') and Sarah ('princess'), sealing the covenant promise.

title: What did Abraham call the place where the ram was provided?
answer: Jehovah-jireh — 'the LORD will provide' or 'in the mount of the LORD it shall be seen.'

title: What did Jacob see at Bethel, and what did he call the place?
answer: A ladder set up to heaven with angels ascending and descending; he called it the house of God and gate of heaven.
note: Jesus applies the image to himself in John 1:51 — he is the meeting point of heaven and earth.

title: What new name was Jacob given after wrestling at Peniel?
answer: Israel, 'for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed.'

title: How did Joseph interpret his brothers' evil against him?
answer: 'Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.'
note: The clearest Old Testament statement of concurrence: the same event is genuinely human wickedness and genuinely divine providence.

title: What blessing of Judah is read as messianic?
answer: 'The sceptre shall not depart from Judah... until Shiloh come.'

title: What were the names of Moses' brother and sister?
answer: Aaron and Miriam.

title: What did Moses' rod become before Pharaoh?
answer: A serpent, which swallowed the serpents of the magicians.

title: Which plague did the Egyptian magicians fail to duplicate?
answer: The third — lice — at which they said, 'This is the finger of God.'

title: What was Israel to do with the Passover lamb's bones?
answer: Break none of them.
note: John cites this as fulfilled at the cross when the soldiers did not break Jesus' legs (John 19:36).

title: What song did Israel sing after crossing the Red Sea?
answer: The Song of Moses — 'I will sing unto the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously.'

title: Who advised Moses to appoint rulers over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens?
answer: Jethro, his father in law, priest of Midian.

title: What did God call Israel at Sinai before giving the Law?
answer: A kingdom of priests and an holy nation, a peculiar treasure above all people.
note: 1 Peter 2:9 transfers this language directly to the Church.

title: What was written on the high priest's mitre plate?
answer: 'HOLINESS TO THE LORD.'

title: What did Moses ask to see, and what was he shown?
answer: God's glory; he was hidden in a cleft of the rock and saw God's 'back parts.'

title: What happened to Moses' face after speaking with God?
answer: It shone, so he veiled it before the people.
note: Paul reads the veil in 2 Cor 3 as the fading glory of the old covenant compared with the abiding glory of the new.

title: What was the scapegoat, and what did it do?
answer: The goat 'for Azazel,' sent alive into the wilderness bearing the people's iniquities.

title: What great command of neighbour-love is found in Leviticus?
answer: 'Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.'

title: What did the law require regarding the poor and the harvest?
answer: Do not reap the corners or glean; leave them for the poor and the stranger.

title: What was the Nazirite vow?
answer: Abstaining from wine, avoiding the dead, and leaving the hair uncut for the vow's duration.

title: Whose rod budded to confirm his priesthood?
answer: Aaron's — it budded, blossomed and yielded almonds.

title: Which prophet was hired to curse Israel but blessed them instead?
answer: Balaam, son of Beor.
note: The New Testament makes Balaam a byword three times — for greed (2 Pet 2:15), error (Jude 11), and teaching Israel to sin (Rev 2:14).

title: What star and sceptre did Balaam foresee?
answer: 'There shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel.'

title: What were the cities of refuge for?
answer: Asylum for one who killed a person unawares, until judgment before the congregation.

title: What did Deuteronomy command parents to do with God's words?
answer: Teach them diligently to children, talking of them at home, walking, lying down, and rising up.

title: By what does man live, according to Deuteronomy 8?
answer: 'Not by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD.'
note: Jesus quotes precisely this verse to answer the first temptation (Matt 4:4).

title: What does Deuteronomy say about the secret things?
answer: 'The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us.'

title: What image describes God's care in the Song of Moses?
answer: An eagle stirring up her nest, bearing her young on her wings.

title: What are the 'everlasting arms' text and its promise?
answer: 'The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms.'

title: What does the Hebrew word 'bara' signify in Genesis 1:1?
answer: A creating whose subject is only ever God — never used of human making.
note: The verb's exclusive divine subject is the grammatical backbone of creatio ex nihilo: the text reserves a category of causation to God alone.

title: What does the plural 'Let us make man' indicate?
answer: A divine self-deliberation; Christians have read it as an early intimation of plurality within God.
note: Jewish readings propose a heavenly court or a plural of majesty. The Christian reading is not that the verse proves the Trinity, but that it leaves room the New Testament later fills.

title: What dominion mandate is given to humanity?
answer: To be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, subdue it and have dominion over living things.
note: Called the cultural mandate: dominion is stewardship under God, not licence. Gen 2:15 glosses it as 'to dress it and to keep it' — cultivate and guard.

title: What is the first thing in Scripture called holy?
answer: Not a place or a person but a time — the seventh day.
note: Sanctity begins with time rather than space, which is why Sabbath precedes tabernacle in the canon's logic.

title: What does the name 'Eve' mean, and when was it given?
answer: 'Living' — given after the fall, as an act of faith in the promise of seed.
note: Adam names her 'living' immediately after being sentenced to death: the naming is itself a confession that Gen 3:15 will hold.

title: What did God make for Adam and Eve, and what did it cost?
answer: Coats of skins — requiring the death of an animal.
note: The first recorded death in Scripture is a substitution to cover human shame, establishing the pattern the sacrificial system will formalise.

title: What guarded the way to the tree of life?
answer: Cherubim and a flaming sword which turned every way.
note: Cherubim reappear woven into the tabernacle veil — the same guardians, now embroidered on the curtain that Christ's death tears open.

title: What did Lamech boast to his wives?
answer: That he would be avenged seventy and sevenfold for wounding a man.
note: Jesus deliberately inverts Lamech's arithmetic in Matt 18:22 — seventy times seven of forgiveness against seventy-sevenfold of vengeance.

title: When did men begin to call upon the name of the LORD?
answer: In the days of Enos, son of Seth.
note: Corporate worship appears in the Sethite line as the counterpoint to the Cainite line's city-building and violence.

title: What was God's assessment of humanity before the flood?
answer: That every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.
note: The verse is the Old Testament's strongest statement of total depravity: the corruption is inward, comprehensive and unremitting.

title: What did God covenant never to do again after the flood?
answer: Never again to curse the ground for man's sake or smite every living thing.
note: The Noahic covenant is unilateral and universal — made with all flesh, not with a chosen line, and grounding common grace.

title: What sanction protects human life in the Noahic covenant?
answer: Whoever sheds man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed — for in the image of God made he man.
note: The reason given is the imago Dei, not social utility, which is why this verse anchors most Christian bioethics.

title: How does Genesis describe Abram's departure from Ur?
answer: He went out not knowing whither he went, at God's call.
note: Hebrews makes this the definition of faith in action: obedience preceding information.

title: What did Abraham do when God announced Sodom's judgment?
answer: He interceded, bargaining from fifty righteous down to ten.
note: The first extended intercession in Scripture, and it appeals to God's own character: 'Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?'

title: What was Sodom's sin, according to Ezekiel?
answer: Pride, fulness of bread, abundance of idleness, and neglect of the poor and needy.
note: Ezekiel's summary is regularly overlooked in popular preaching, which tends to isolate Gen 19 from its canonical commentary.

title: What test did God give Abraham on Moriah?
answer: To offer Isaac, his only son, as a burnt offering.
note: The first occurrence of the word 'love' in the Bible is here — of a father for a son he is asked to give up, which the New Testament reads typologically.

title: Why did Jacob's ladder vision matter for Israel's self-understanding?
answer: It located God's presence at an ordinary place, unearned and unexpected.
note: 'Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not' — the theology of presence that later attaches to tabernacle, temple and finally to Christ.

title: What does 'Immanuel' theology begin with in Exodus?
answer: God's declared intention to dwell among his people.
note: 'Let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them' — the tabernacle's purpose is proximity, which John 1:14 fulfils with 'tabernacled among us.'

title: Why did God harden Pharaoh's heart?
answer: To display his power and make his name known throughout the earth.
note: Exodus alternates: Pharaoh hardens his own heart in the early plagues, God hardens it later — the text refuses a single simple causality.

title: What is the theological significance of the Passover being a memorial?
answer: Each generation recounts the exodus as though personally delivered.
note: 'This is done because of that which the LORD did unto me' — biblical memory is participatory, which shapes the church's understanding of the Lord's Supper.

title: What did God say about the firstborn after the exodus?
answer: That every firstborn in Israel was his, redeemed by a substitute.
note: Redemption by substitution is built into Israel's family law before it is systematised in Levitical sacrifice.

title: What was the bread of the Presence?
answer: Twelve loaves set before the LORD continually, one for each tribe.
note: David's eating of it (1 Sam 21) becomes Jesus' argument that mercy outranks ritual (Matt 12:3-7).

title: What made a sacrifice acceptable in Leviticus?
answer: That it be without blemish, offered willingly at the appointed place.
note: 1 Peter 1:19 applies the same phrase to Christ — 'a lamb without blemish and without spot' — making the Levitical standard a christological criterion.

title: What is the meaning of 'atonement' (kaphar) in Hebrew?
answer: To cover, and by extension to ransom or wipe away.
note: The related noun kapporeth names the mercy seat: the place of covering is where blood is applied, which is why Rom 3:25 calls Christ the hilasterion.

title: Why was the tabernacle built to a heavenly pattern?
answer: Moses was to make all things after the pattern shewed him in the mount.
note: Hebrews 8:5 builds an entire argument on this: earthly worship is a shadow of a heavenly reality, so the new covenant is not innovation but arrival.

title: What did the trumpet of Jubilee proclaim?
answer: Liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants.
note: Isaiah 61 and Luke 4 take up Jubilee language for the Messiah's ministry — release, not merely forgiveness, is the register.

title: What was the sin of presumption in Numbers?
answer: Sinning 'with a high hand' — defiant, deliberate rebellion, for which no sacrifice was appointed.
note: The distinction between inadvertent and defiant sin lies behind Heb 10:26 and the later Catholic distinction of mortal and venial sin.

title: What does the census in Numbers signify theologically?
answer: That God's people are counted and known, ordered for both worship and warfare.
note: The book's Hebrew name is Bemidbar, 'in the wilderness' — the counting frames a story about who survives the journey.

title: What did Moses say when told to restrain Eldad and Medad?
answer: 'Would God that all the LORD's people were prophets.'
note: Joel 2:28 and Acts 2 answer Moses' wish directly: the Spirit poured on all flesh is the fulfilment of this unfulfilled longing.

title: What was the water of separation with the red heifer for?
answer: Purifying those defiled by contact with the dead.
note: Hebrews 9:13-14 argues from lesser to greater: if ashes purify the flesh, how much more Christ's blood purges the conscience.

title: What law of witnesses does Deuteronomy establish?
answer: At the mouth of two or three witnesses shall a matter be established.
note: Carried directly into church discipline (Matt 18:16), apostolic practice (2 Cor 13:1), and the protection of elders (1 Tim 5:19).

title: What does Deuteronomy say about a hanged man?
answer: He that is hanged is accursed of God, and must be buried the same day.
note: Paul cites this in Gal 3:13: Christ was made a curse for us, taking the covenantal curse onto himself at the tree.

title: What was the law of the king in Deuteronomy?
answer: He must not multiply horses, wives or silver, and must write his own copy of the law.
note: Solomon violates all three prohibitions in 1 Kgs 10-11 — the narrative is written as a deliberate indictment against this statute.

title: What are the blessings and curses of Deuteronomy 28?
answer: Blessing for obedience and a far longer catalogue of curses for covenant breach.
note: The disproportion is intentional: the exile the prophets later announce is not improvised judgment but the covenant's own published terms.

title: What does 'circumcise the foreskin of your heart' mean?
answer: That the outward covenant sign must be matched by inward devotion.
note: Deut 30:6 promises God himself will perform the circumcision — grace precedes and enables the obedience the law demands, anticipating Jer 31 and Rom 2:29.

title: What was God's repeated charge to Joshua at his commissioning?
answer: "Be strong and of a good courage" — grounded in God's presence, not Joshua's ability.
note: 'Be strong and of a good courage' occurs four times in Joshua 1, and each time it is grounded not in Joshua's capacity but in God's presence and in the written word he is to meditate on.

title: Who hid the spies in Jericho, and what became of her?
answer: Rahab the harlot; she was spared and became an ancestor of David and of Christ.
note: Named for faith in Heb 11:31 and for works in Jas 2:25 — the same act read two ways.

title: What marked Rahab's house for deliverance?
answer: A scarlet cord bound in the window.

title: How did Israel cross the Jordan?
answer: The waters stood in a heap when the priests bearing the Ark stepped in.
note: The waters stood back when the priests' feet touched them, not before — the sign followed the step, reversing the usual order of evidence and obedience.

title: Why did Israel lose the battle at Ai?
answer: Achan's hidden sin — he took of the devoted spoil of Jericho.
note: One man's hidden sin brought corporate defeat, and Joshua 7:11 says 'Israel hath sinned' — the individual act is attributed to the whole body, a solidarity assumed throughout the Old Testament.

title: Which people deceived Israel into a treaty?
answer: The Gibeonites, with mouldy bread and worn clothes, feigning a long journey.
note: Israel failed because they "asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD" (v.14).

title: What was Joshua's final challenge to Israel?
answer: "Choose you this day whom ye will serve... as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD."
note: 'Choose you this day whom ye will serve' assumes the real possibility of covenant abandonment, and Joshua's warning in 24:19 — 'ye cannot serve the LORD' — is startlingly pessimistic about their capacity.

title: What cycle repeats throughout the book of Judges?
answer: Sin, servitude, supplication, salvation — then relapse.

title: What verse twice summarises the moral state of the Judges era?
answer: "There was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes."

title: Who was the only female judge of Israel?
answer: Deborah, who judged under a palm tree and went with Barak to battle.
note: Deborah is called both prophetess and judge, and Barak's refusal to go without her results in the honour going to a woman — the narrative treats this as a rebuke to him, not to her.

title: How large was Gideon's final army, and why?
answer: 300 men — so Israel could not boast that its own hand had saved it.

title: What was the source of Samson's strength?
answer: The Spirit of the LORD, tied to his Nazirite vow — symbolised in his unshorn hair.
note: His strength was tied to the Nazirite vow rather than to his hair as such; the hair was the visible sign of consecration, and Judges 16:20 records that 'he wist not that the LORD was departed from him.'

title: What famous pledge did Ruth make to Naomi?
answer: "Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God."
note: 'Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God' is a conversion as much as a family commitment, and it explains why a Moabitess enters the messianic line without difficulty.

title: What is a kinsman-redeemer (goel)?
answer: A near relative who could buy back family land, redeem a relative from slavery, and raise up an heir — Boaz's role for Ruth.
note: One of the clearest Old Testament pictures of redemption in Christ.

title: How is Ruth connected to Christ?
answer: She was the great-grandmother of David and appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus.

title: Who was Hannah, and what did she vow?
answer: Samuel's mother, who vowed to give her son to the LORD all the days of his life.

title: How did young Samuel answer God's call?
answer: "Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth."
note: 'Speak; for thy servant heareth' comes after three failures to recognise the voice, and 1 Samuel 3:1 notes that 'the word of the LORD was precious in those days' — recognition had to be taught.

title: Why did Israel demand a king, and how did God read the request?
answer: To be like the nations; God told Samuel, "they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them."

title: What word did Samuel speak to Saul about sacrifice?
answer: "To obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams."
note: 'To obey is better than sacrifice' (1 Sam 15:22) is echoed by Hosea, Micah, the Psalms and Jesus himself — one of the Old Testament's most persistent refrains against ritual without submission.

title: By what standard did God choose David?
answer: "Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart."

title: With what did David face Goliath?
answer: A sling and five smooth stones — and "the name of the LORD of hosts."
note: David's speech in 1 Samuel 17:45-47 makes the theological point explicit: the battle is the LORD's, and the outcome is so 'that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel.'

title: Who was David's covenant friend, and why is he remembered?
answer: Jonathan, Saul's son, who loved David as his own soul and yielded his own claim to the throne.

title: What was the Davidic covenant?
answer: God's promise that David's house, kingdom and throne would be established for ever.
note: The root of Messianic expectation: Gabriel echoes it to Mary in Luke 1:32-33.

title: How did Nathan confront David over Bathsheba?
answer: With the parable of the poor man's ewe lamb, then: "Thou art the man."
note: The parable made David pronounce sentence on himself before 'Thou art the man' landed — indirect narrative disarms the defences that direct accusation would have raised.

title: Which psalm records David's repentance after that sin?
answer: Psalm 51 — "Create in me a clean heart, O God."
note: Psalm 51 asks God to blot out, wash and cleanse — three verbs for one need — and confesses 'against thee, thee only, have I sinned,' recognising that all wrongdoing is ultimately theological.

title: Which of David's sons rebelled and seized the throne?
answer: Absalom, who died caught by his head in an oak.

title: What did Solomon ask God for, and what did he receive besides?
answer: An understanding heart to judge; God added riches and honour.
note: He asked for an understanding heart to discern between good and bad, and 1 Kings 3:10 says the request itself pleased the Lord — what we ask for reveals what we value.

title: What caused the kingdom to divide after Solomon?
answer: Solomon's idolatry, and Rehoboam's harsh answer to Israel's plea for lighter burdens.
note: 1 Kings 11 attributes it to Solomon's idolatry through foreign wives, and 12:15 adds that the split was 'from the LORD' — human folly and divine purpose named in the same narrative.

title: Name the two kingdoms after the split and their capitals.
answer: Israel (ten northern tribes), capital Samaria; Judah (south), capital Jerusalem.

title: What contest did Elijah hold on Mount Carmel?
answer: A test of whose God answers by fire, against 450 prophets of Baal.

title: How did God speak to Elijah at Horeb?
answer: Not in wind, earthquake or fire, but in "a still small voice."
note: Elijah is sent to the same mountain where Moses met God, and the question 'What doest thou here, Elijah?' is asked twice without ever being answered — God addresses the despair by giving him work and a successor.

title: What did Elisha ask of Elijah before his departure?
answer: A double portion of Elijah's spirit — the firstborn's inheritance.

title: How was Naaman the Syrian healed of leprosy?
answer: By dipping seven times in the Jordan at Elisha's word, after resisting its simplicity.
note: Jesus cites Naaman to show God's mercy reaching beyond Israel (Luke 4:27).

title: Which king was healed and given fifteen added years?
answer: Hezekiah, with the shadow turned back ten degrees as a sign.
note: Hezekiah's added years produced Manasseh, Judah's worst king, born three years into the extension — the narrative leaves the reader to draw the uncomfortable inference.

title: Which boy king led a great reformation after the Book of the Law was found?
answer: Josiah, who began to reign at eight years old.

title: Who destroyed Jerusalem and the temple, and in what year?
answer: Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, in 586 BC.
note: 586 BC ends the Davidic monarchy and raises the question that dominates the exilic prophets: whether God's promises to David had failed.

title: Which king's decree allowed the Jews to return and rebuild?
answer: Cyrus of Persia.
note: Named by Isaiah roughly 150 years earlier (Isa 44:28; 45:1).

title: Who led the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls, and in how many days?
answer: Nehemiah — fifty-two days.

title: Which book of the Bible never mentions God by name?
answer: Esther — though his providence pervades the story.
note: "Who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"

title: What book was Joshua told to meditate in day and night?
answer: The book of the law, that he might observe to do all written therein.

title: Whom did Joshua meet with a drawn sword near Jericho?
answer: The captain of the host of the LORD, before whom Joshua fell and worshipped.

title: How many days did Israel compass Jericho, and how many times on the last day?
answer: Six days once daily, and seven times on the seventh day.

title: Who took the accursed thing at Jericho?
answer: Achan of the tribe of Judah — a Babylonish garment, silver, and a wedge of gold.

title: What did Joshua ask of God during the battle at Gibeon?
answer: That the sun stand still upon Gibeon and the moon in the valley of Ajalon.

title: Which aged man asked for the hill country at eighty-five?
answer: Caleb — 'Give me this mountain.'

title: Which tribe received no land inheritance, and why?
answer: Levi — the LORD God of Israel was their inheritance, sustained by offerings.

title: What did Gideon's three hundred carry into battle?
answer: Trumpets, and empty pitchers with lamps inside.
note: Paul's 'treasure in earthen vessels' (2 Cor 4:7) works the same logic: the vessel must break for the light to show.

title: Which judge made a rash vow concerning what came out of his house?
answer: Jephthah the Gileadite.

title: Who betrayed Samson, and how did he die?
answer: Delilah; he died pulling down the pillars of Dagon's temple on the Philistines.

title: Who were Ruth's son, grandson and great-grandson?
answer: Obed, Jesse, and David.

title: What happened to Eli's sons, and to Eli?
answer: Hophni and Phinehas were slain and the ark taken; Eli fell backward and died at the news.

title: What name did the dying wife of Phinehas give her son?
answer: Ichabod — 'the glory is departed from Israel.'

title: What stone did Samuel set up, and what did it mean?
answer: Ebenezer — 'Hitherto hath the LORD helped us.'

title: How did Saul's disobedience about Amalek end?
answer: God rejected him from being king; Samuel said obedience is better than sacrifice.

title: How did David soothe Saul's troubled spirit?
answer: By playing the harp.

title: Why did David refuse to strike Saul in the cave?
answer: Because Saul was the LORD's anointed.

title: Whom did Saul consult at Endor?
answer: A woman with a familiar spirit, seeking Samuel.

title: Who died when he touched the ark, and why?
answer: Uzzah — he steadied it contrary to God's prescribed manner of carrying it.
note: 1 Chron 15:13 supplies the reason: they had not sought God 'after the due order.'

title: How did David behave as the ark entered Jerusalem?
answer: He danced before the LORD with all his might, girded with a linen ephod.

title: What kindness did David show Jonathan's son?
answer: He restored Saul's land to Mephibosheth and set him at the king's table continually.

title: What were David's last words about his house?
answer: God had made with him 'an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things, and sure.'

title: What sin closed David's reign, and what was the consequence?
answer: Numbering the people; a pestilence in which seventy thousand died.

title: What was Solomon's famous judgment?
answer: Ordering the living child divided, exposing the true mother by her compassion.

title: What fed Elijah at the brook Cherith?
answer: Ravens brought him bread and flesh morning and evening.

title: Whose vineyard did Ahab and Jezebel seize?
answer: Naboth the Jezreelite's.

title: How did Elijah depart the earth?
answer: By a chariot of fire and horses of fire, in a whirlwind into heaven.

title: How did Elisha's servant come to see the heavenly army?
answer: Elisha prayed, 'LORD, open his eyes,' and he saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire.

title: What did Hezekiah do with Sennacherib's threatening letter?
answer: He spread it before the LORD in the house of the LORD.

title: Which king reigned fifty-five years and filled Jerusalem with innocent blood?
answer: Manasseh — though 2 Chronicles records his later repentance.

title: What prayer of an obscure man is recorded in Chronicles' genealogies?
answer: The prayer of Jabez, that God would bless him and enlarge his coast.

title: What promise follows 'if my people, which are called by my name'?
answer: '...shall humble themselves, and pray... then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.'

title: What was Ezra's threefold resolve?
answer: To seek the law of the LORD, to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments.

title: How did Nehemiah's builders work under threat?
answer: With one hand at the work and the other holding a weapon.

title: What did Nehemiah say was the people's strength?
answer: 'The joy of the LORD is your strength.'

title: What plea did Mordecai make to Esther?
answer: 'Who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?'

title: What feast commemorates Esther's deliverance?
answer: Purim, named from the 'pur' or lot Haman cast.

title: What theological pattern governs the book of Judges?
answer: Sin, servitude, supplication, salvation, silence — then repetition.
note: The spiral descends rather than circles: each cycle leaves Israel worse than the last, arguing structurally for the need of a righteous king.

title: What is the significance of Samuel being both prophet and judge?
answer: He is the hinge between the era of judges and the monarchy.
note: Samuel anoints two kings but crowns no dynasty of his own — prophetic office stands over royal office from the monarchy's first day.

title: Why does the ark narrative matter theologically?
answer: It shows God's presence cannot be manipulated as a talisman.
note: Israel carries the ark into battle as a charm and loses; God then defeats Dagon without any Israelite help, proving he needs no defenders.

title: What did Samuel warn the monarchy would cost?
answer: Conscription, taxation, seizure of land, and eventual crying out under the king they chose.
note: Every warning is fulfilled precisely under Solomon and Rehoboam, and the people's cry in 1 Kgs 12:4 echoes the verb of 1 Sam 8:18.

title: What is the theological weight of 1 Samuel 16:7?
answer: 'Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.'
note: Placed between Saul's rejection and David's anointing, it functions as the narrator's stated criterion for the entire history that follows.

title: How does the Davidic covenant reach beyond David?
answer: It promises a house, a throne and a kingdom established for ever.
note: Gabriel quotes this promise almost verbatim to Mary in Luke 1:32-33, presenting Jesus as its terminus rather than merely its heir.

title: What is the significance of Solomon's temple prayer?
answer: He confesses that heaven cannot contain God, much less the house he built.
note: The temple's own dedication prayer denies that God is housed in it, guarding Israel from the pagan notion of a resident local deity.

title: What did Solomon anticipate about the foreigner?
answer: That the stranger from a far country would come and pray toward the house, and God would hear.
note: Gentile inclusion is built into the temple's founding charter — which is why Jesus' cleansing quotes 'a house of prayer for all nations' (Isa 56:7).

title: What was the theological issue at Mount Carmel?
answer: Not whether God exists but which God is God — the people 'halted between two opinions.'
note: Syncretism, not atheism, is the biblical world's characteristic unbelief; Elijah forces a decision the people had been avoiding.

title: Why is the 'still small voice' significant?
answer: God was not in the wind, earthquake or fire, but in a low whisper.
note: Coming immediately after Carmel's fire, it corrects the assumption that God's normal mode is spectacle.

title: What is the theological function of the Elisha miracle cycle?
answer: To show God's care extending to the poor, the foreign and the ordinary.
note: Jesus cites Elijah's widow and Naaman the Syrian at Nazareth (Luke 4:25-27) precisely to argue for Gentile inclusion — and is nearly killed for it.

title: What did the northern kingdom never have?
answer: A single good king; every one of the nineteen walked in the sins of Jeroboam.
note: The verdict formula is repeated relentlessly, making the fall of Samaria in 722 BC read as inevitable rather than tragic accident.

title: Why did the northern kingdom fall, according to 2 Kings 17?
answer: Because they feared other gods and rejected God's statutes and covenant.
note: The chapter is the narrator's one extended theological essay, explaining exile in covenantal rather than political terms.

title: What reform did Josiah carry out?
answer: He destroyed the high places, defiled Topheth, and kept a Passover unequalled since the judges.
note: Yet 2 Kgs 23:26 says the LORD did not turn from his wrath — a sobering note that reform delayed but did not cancel judgment.

title: What is Chronicles' distinctive perspective?
answer: It retells the history from a priestly, temple-centred and Davidic viewpoint for the returned exiles.
note: Chronicles omits David's adultery and Israel's northern kings — not concealment but selection, since its question is 'who are we now?' not 'what went wrong?'

title: How does Chronicles end, and why does it matter?
answer: With Cyrus' decree and the words 'let him go up' — an open door, not a closed exile.
note: In the Hebrew canon this is the last verse of the Old Testament, so the Hebrew Bible ends with a summons to return home.

title: What opposition did the returned exiles face?
answer: Discouragement, hired counsellors, false accusation to the king, and mockery.
note: The pattern of external ridicule then internal compromise recurs; Nehemiah's answer is prayer plus practical guard duty, refusing to choose between them.

title: What crisis did Ezra confront on arriving?
answer: Intermarriage with surrounding peoples, threatening the community's covenant identity.
note: The concern is religious, not ethnic — Ruth the Moabitess is a celebrated ancestor of David, having confessed Israel's God.

title: What happened when the Law was read at the Water Gate?
answer: The people wept, then were told the day was holy and the joy of the LORD was their strength.
note: The Levites 'gave the sense, and caused them to understand' — the first clear picture of expository preaching and translation in Scripture.

title: What is remarkable about God's absence from Esther?
answer: His name never appears, yet providence saturates the plot.
note: The king's sleepless night is the book's hinge, and no cause is given — the narrative technique itself argues for hidden providence.

title: How long did Nehemiah's wall take, and what did the nations conclude?
answer: Fifty-two days; the surrounding nations perceived the work was wrought of God.
note: The enemies themselves supply the theological verdict, which is the narrator's preferred method of proof.

title: What covenant renewal did Nehemiah lead?
answer: A sealed written agreement to keep the law, the sabbath, the tithes and the temple service.
note: Nehemiah 9's prayer is the Old Testament's longest historical confession, retelling the whole story as a case study in God's patience.

title: What abuse did Nehemiah confront among his own people?
answer: Usury and the enslavement of Jewish brethren by Jewish nobles during famine.
note: He renounces his own governor's allowance as a matter of credibility — reform of others is preceded by cost to himself.

title: What question drives the book of Job?
answer: Whether a man will serve God for nothing — that is, whether faith is genuine apart from reward.

title: What did Job confess after losing everything?
answer: "The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."

title: What hope did Job express in the midst of suffering?
answer: "I know that my redeemer liveth... yet from my flesh shall I see God."

title: How did God finally answer Job?
answer: Not with explanations but with questions out of the whirlwind about creation's vastness.

title: How many psalms are there, and into how many books are they divided?
answer: 150 psalms, in five books, each closing with a doxology.

title: What is the longest chapter in the Bible, and what is its theme?
answer: Psalm 119, 176 verses — an acrostic celebrating the word of God.

title: Which psalm is quoted from the cross?
answer: Psalm 22 — "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"
note: It also foretells pierced hands and feet and casting lots for garments (vv.16-18).

title: Which psalm is the most quoted in the New Testament?
answer: Psalm 110 — "The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand."

title: What are the "Songs of Ascents"?
answer: Psalms 120-134, sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem for the feasts.

title: What is an imprecatory psalm?
answer: A psalm calling down God's judgment on enemies, entrusting vengeance to God rather than taking it.
note: Paul's counterpart: "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Rom 12:19).

title: What is the stated purpose of Proverbs?
answer: To know wisdom and instruction, and to give subtlety to the simple and discretion to the young.

title: What is the "beginning of knowledge" according to Proverbs?
answer: The fear of the LORD.

title: What does Proverbs 3:5-6 counsel?
answer: Trust in the LORD with all thine heart, lean not on thine own understanding, and he shall direct thy paths.

title: What seven things does the LORD hate, per Proverbs 6?
answer: Proud eyes, a lying tongue, hands shedding innocent blood, a wicked heart, feet swift to mischief, a false witness, and one who sows discord.

title: How does Proverbs personify wisdom?
answer: As a woman calling in the streets, present with God before creation.
note: Early Christian writers read Proverbs 8 alongside John 1 and Colossians 1.

title: What does Proverbs 31 describe?
answer: The virtuous woman, an acrostic portrait praising a woman who fears the LORD above charm and beauty.

title: What Hebrew word opens and closes Ecclesiastes, and what does it mean?
answer: "Hevel" — vapour, breath, fleeting; rendered "vanity."

title: What phrase marks the limited horizon Ecclesiastes examines?
answer: "Under the sun" — life reckoned without reference to God.

title: What is the conclusion of the whole matter in Ecclesiastes?
answer: "Fear God, and keep his commandments; for this is the whole duty of man."

title: What does Ecclesiastes 3 famously teach about time?
answer: There is a season and a time to every purpose under heaven.

title: What has God set in the human heart, according to Ecclesiastes?
answer: Eternity ("the world") — so nothing temporal can satisfy.

title: How does the Song of Solomon describe the strength of love?
answer: "Love is strong as death... many waters cannot quench love."

title: Which canonical book never names God directly besides Esther?
answer: The Song of Solomon.

title: What three readings of the Song have circulated since antiquity?
answer: A literal celebration of marital love; an allegory of God's love for Israel; and an allegory of Christ's love for the Church.

title: Who challenged God concerning Job, and under what limits?
answer: Satan, permitted to touch Job's possessions and body but not his life.

title: How did Job's latter end compare with his beginning?
answer: The LORD blessed his latter end more than his beginning, doubling his substance.

title: What does Psalm 1 contrast?
answer: The blessed man rooted like a tree by rivers of water, and the ungodly like driven chaff.

title: What does Psalm 8 ask about humanity?
answer: 'What is man, that thou art mindful of him?'
note: Hebrews 2 reads the psalm christologically: we do not yet see all things under man, but we see Jesus crowned.

title: Which psalm begins 'The heavens declare the glory of God'?
answer: Psalm 19, which then turns from creation's witness to the perfect law of the LORD.

title: What does Psalm 23 say the LORD prepares?
answer: 'A table before me in the presence of mine enemies.'

title: What does Psalm 46 counsel amid upheaval?
answer: 'Be still, and know that I am God.'

title: What sacrifices does Psalm 51 say God will not despise?
answer: 'A broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart.'

title: What does Psalm 90, attributed to Moses, ask?
answer: 'So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.'

title: What promise does Psalm 91 give to the one who dwells in the secret place?
answer: He shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty, covered with God's feathers.

title: How far has God removed our transgressions, per Psalm 103?
answer: 'As far as the east is from the west.'

title: Which psalm verse does the New Testament apply to Christ's session?
answer: 'The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand.'
note: Jesus uses it to press the Pharisees on Messiah's identity (Matt 22:44), and it recurs throughout Hebrews.

title: What does Psalm 119:105 call God's word?
answer: 'A lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.'

title: What does Psalm 133 praise?
answer: How good and pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.

title: What does Psalm 139 say about God's knowledge of us?
answer: He searched and knew us, beset us behind and before, and formed us in the womb.

title: How does the Psalter close?
answer: With Psalm 150 — 'Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD.'

title: What does Proverbs say about a soft answer?
answer: 'A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.'

title: What goes before destruction, per Proverbs?
answer: 'Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.'

title: What friend does Proverbs describe as sticking closer than a brother?
answer: A true friend, contrasted with many nominal companions.

title: What does Proverbs say about training a child?
answer: 'Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.'

title: What happens where there is no vision?
answer: 'The people perish' — literally cast off restraint, where there is no prophetic revelation.

title: What two things did Agur ask of God?
answer: Remove falsehood far from him, and give him neither poverty nor riches.

title: What does Ecclesiastes say about two being better than one?
answer: They have a good reward; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

title: What does Ecclesiastes counsel the young?
answer: 'Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth.'

title: What refrain warns against awakening love prematurely?
answer: 'Stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.'

title: How does the Song describe the mutual belonging of the lovers?
answer: 'My beloved is mine, and I am his.'

title: What does the Song say many waters cannot do?
answer: They cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.

title: What is the structural problem the book of Job sets up?
answer: The reader knows what Job never learns — that his suffering is not punishment.
note: The prologue's dramatic irony means the friends' theology is refuted before they open their mouths; the book critiques retribution theology from the inside.

title: What is the accuser's actual charge in Job?
answer: Not that Job is wicked, but that piety is self-interested — 'Doth Job fear God for nought?'
note: The question at stake is whether disinterested love of God is possible, which makes Job a book about worship before it is a book about pain.

title: What does Job say about his Redeemer?
answer: 'I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth.'
note: The Hebrew 'goel' is the kinsman-redeemer of Ruth and Leviticus — Job asks for a family member with legal standing to vindicate him.

title: How does God's speech from the whirlwind answer Job?
answer: With questions about creation rather than explanations of suffering.
note: God never tells Job about the wager. The answer to the problem of pain in Job is a person, not a proposition.

title: What does God say about the friends at the end?
answer: That they had not spoken of him what is right, as his servant Job had.
note: Startling, since Job accused God repeatedly while the friends defended him — honest complaint is vindicated over dishonest orthodoxy.

title: What are the five books of the Psalter, and how does each end?
answer: Each of the five books closes with a doxology, the last being all of Psalm 150.
note: The fivefold division deliberately mirrors the Pentateuch, presenting the Psalter as Israel's sung Torah.

title: What are the royal psalms, and how are they read?
answer: Psalms about the Davidic king, read messianically after the monarchy's failure.
note: Psalm 2 is quoted at Jesus' baptism, in Acts 4, and in Hebrews 1 — the church read the throne psalms as unfulfilled until Christ.

title: What is a lament psalm's typical structure?
answer: Address, complaint, petition, and usually a vow of praise or statement of trust.
note: Roughly a third of the Psalter is lament, which is why a worship diet of only celebration is biblically unbalanced.

title: Which psalm ends without resolution?
answer: Psalm 88 — its last word is 'darkness,' with no turn to praise.
note: Its presence in the canon means Scripture makes room for unresolved grief, refusing to require a tidy ending from the sufferer.

title: What is the theological claim of Psalm 22 for Christians?
answer: It describes pierced hands and feet, parted garments and casting lots, centuries before crucifixion.
note: Jesus' cry of verse 1 from the cross invokes the whole psalm, which ends in worldwide worship — the quotation is not despair but citation.

title: What does Psalm 51 ask God to create?
answer: A clean heart, and a right spirit renewed within.
note: The verb 'create' is bara — the same reserved-for-God verb as Gen 1:1. David asks for nothing less than a new creation.

title: What is the acrostic structure of Psalm 119?
answer: Twenty-two stanzas of eight verses, each stanza beginning with a successive Hebrew letter.
note: The form enacts the content: the whole alphabet is enlisted to praise the Word, suggesting exhaustive devotion from A to Z.

title: What does Proverbs mean by 'the fear of the LORD'?
answer: Reverent submission to God as the starting point of all real knowledge.
note: Wisdom in Proverbs is not intelligence but rightly ordered relationship — which is why a fool can be clever.

title: How should the promises of Proverbs be read?
answer: As general patterns of how life usually works, not as unconditional guarantees.
note: Job and Ecclesiastes exist in the canon precisely to prevent Proverbs from being read as a mechanical formula.

title: What role does Lady Wisdom play in Proverbs 8?
answer: She was with God before creation, rejoicing in the habitable earth.
note: The passage was central to the Arian controversy — Arius read 'the LORD possessed me' as 'created me' to argue the Son was a creature; Nicaea rejected that reading.

title: What does Ecclesiastes mean by 'hevel'?
answer: Vapour, breath, mist — the fleeting and ungraspable rather than the merely worthless.
note: 'Vanity' in English misleads. Qoheleth's complaint is that life will not sit still to be mastered, not that it has no value.

title: What is Ecclesiastes' repeated positive counsel?
answer: Eat your bread, drink your wine, and enjoy your labour as God's gift.
note: The refrain occurs seven times. Beneath the sceptical surface is a robust doctrine of receiving ordinary life as grace.

title: How does Ecclesiastes describe old age and death?
answer: In an extended allegory of a failing house, ending with the silver cord loosed.
note: 'The spirit shall return unto God who gave it' — Qoheleth's horizon opens at the very end, beyond the 'under the sun' limit he set himself.

title: Why is the Song of Solomon in the canon?
answer: It affirms embodied married love as good, and has been read as picturing divine love.
note: Rabbi Akiba called it the Holy of Holies among the writings. Its inclusion refuses the ascetic suspicion that bodily love is sub-spiritual.

title: What does the Song say love is stronger than?
answer: Death; and jealousy is cruel as the grave, its coals a most vehement flame.
note: 'A very flame of the LORD' — the only place the divine name appears in the book, and it appears as the source of love's fire.

title: What distinguishes the Major from the Minor Prophets?
answer: Length only — Isaiah through Daniel are longer books, not more important ones.

title: What did Isaiah see in the year King Uzziah died?
answer: The Lord high and lifted up, with seraphim crying "Holy, holy, holy."
note: The earthly throne had just been vacated, and Isaiah sees the true throne occupied; John 12:41 says Isaiah 'saw his glory, and spake of him' — of Christ.

title: How did Isaiah respond to that vision, and how was he cleansed?
answer: "Woe is me! for I am undone" — then a live coal from the altar touched his lips.

title: What names does Isaiah 9 give the promised child?
answer: Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.
note: 'The mighty God' and 'The everlasting Father' are titles no Israelite would apply to a merely human king, which is why the verse presses the question of the child's identity.

title: What comes forth from the stem of Jesse?
answer: A rod and a Branch, on whom the Spirit of the LORD shall rest.

title: What are the four "Servant Songs" of Isaiah?
answer: Isaiah 42, 49, 50 and 52:13-53:12 — portraits of the LORD's suffering, obedient Servant.

title: What does Isaiah 53 say the Servant bore?
answer: Our griefs and sorrows; he was wounded for our transgressions, and with his stripes we are healed.
note: Philip preaches Christ to the Ethiopian from this very chapter (Acts 8:32-35).

title: What promise does Isaiah 40 give the weary?
answer: They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength and mount up with wings as eagles.
note: The progression is deliberate and descending — mount up, run, walk — ending with the least dramatic and hardest: to walk and not faint.

title: How old was Jeremiah when called, and what was his objection?
answer: A youth — "I cannot speak: for I am a child."

title: When did God say he knew Jeremiah?
answer: Before he formed him in the belly, and sanctified him before birth.
note: 'Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee' grounds vocation in divine choice preceding existence, and the verse has become central to Christian arguments about the unborn.

title: Why is Jeremiah called the weeping prophet?
answer: He wept over Judah's obstinacy and the coming destruction of Jerusalem.

title: What did the potter's house teach Jeremiah?
answer: That God as potter may reshape a nation as clay in his hand.

title: How long did Jeremiah say the Babylonian exile would last?
answer: Seventy years.
note: Daniel is reading this very prophecy when he prays in Daniel 9:2.

title: What is the New Covenant Jeremiah foretold?
answer: God's law written on the heart, all knowing him, and sins remembered no more.
note: Quoted in full in Hebrews 8:8-12 as fulfilled in Christ.

title: What great affirmation stands at the centre of Lamentations?
answer: "His compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness."
note: Lamentations 3:22-23 sits at the exact centre of a five-chapter acrostic structure — the hope is placed architecturally at the heart of the grief.

title: What did Ezekiel see in his opening vision?
answer: The glory of God on a heavenly throne-chariot with four living creatures and wheels within wheels.

title: What was Ezekiel called to be, and what did it require?
answer: A watchman to the house of Israel, accountable to warn them.

title: What did the vision of the valley of dry bones signify?
answer: The resurrection and restoration of the whole house of Israel by God's Spirit.
note: Ezekiel is asked 'can these bones live?' and answers 'thou knowest' — refusing both presumption and unbelief, which the text treats as the right response.

title: What heart transplant does Ezekiel promise?
answer: A new heart and a new spirit — the stony heart removed, a heart of flesh given.

title: Why did Daniel and his friends refuse the king's food?
answer: Daniel purposed not to defile himself with the king's meat and wine.
note: The issue was probably idolatrous dedication rather than kosher law alone, and Daniel 'purposed in his heart' before the test arrived — resolve preceded pressure.

title: What did Nebuchadnezzar's statue dream represent?
answer: Four successive kingdoms, struck by a stone cut without hands — God's everlasting kingdom.

title: Who appeared with the three Hebrews in the furnace?
answer: A fourth, whose form was "like a son of the gods."

title: What words appeared on Belshazzar's wall, and what did they mean?
answer: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN — numbered, weighed, and divided.

title: How often did Daniel pray, even under the death decree?
answer: Three times a day, toward Jerusalem, with his windows open.

title: Who is the "Son of man" of Daniel 7?
answer: One coming with the clouds of heaven, given everlasting dominion by the Ancient of Days.
note: Jesus' favourite self-designation, cited at his trial (Mark 14:62).

title: What did God tell Hosea his marriage would picture?
answer: Israel's spiritual adultery, and God's costly, pursuing covenant love.

title: What does God desire more than sacrifice, per Hosea?
answer: Mercy, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
note: Jesus quotes it twice against the Pharisees (Matt 9:13; 12:7).

title: Which prophecy of Joel did Peter cite at Pentecost?
answer: "I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy."

title: What does Amos demand instead of empty worship?
answer: "Let judgement roll down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream."

title: What nation does Obadiah address, and why?
answer: Edom, for its pride and its gloating over Jerusalem's calamity.

title: Why did Jonah flee from God's call?
answer: He knew God was gracious and feared Nineveh would repent and be spared.

title: Where did Micah say the Messiah would be born?
answer: Bethlehem Ephratah, "whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting."
note: Micah 5:2 adds that his 'goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting' — a pre-existence claim attached to a birthplace prophecy.

title: What does the LORD require of you, according to Micah?
answer: To do justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with thy God.
note: The three demands are relational rather than ritual, and 'walk humbly with thy God' places the other two inside a relationship rather than a code.

title: What phrase from Habakkuk became a Reformation watchword?
answer: "The just shall live by his faith."
note: Quoted in Rom 1:17, Gal 3:11, and Heb 10:38.

title: How does Habakkuk end?
answer: With a resolve to rejoice in the LORD even if fig tree and flock fail.

title: What did Haggai rebuke the returned exiles for?
answer: Living in panelled houses while the house of the LORD lay waste.

title: What word did Zechariah give Zerubbabel?
answer: "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts."

title: What king does Zechariah 9 foretell?
answer: One coming lowly, riding upon an ass and upon a colt.

title: What price of betrayal does Zechariah name?
answer: Thirty pieces of silver, cast to the potter in the house of the LORD.

title: With what promise does the Old Testament close?
answer: The sending of Elijah the prophet before the great and dreadful day of the LORD.
note: Jesus identifies John the Baptist as this Elijah (Matt 11:14).

title: Which four kings of Judah span Isaiah's ministry?
answer: Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah.

title: What invitation opens Isaiah's argument in chapter 1?
answer: 'Come now, and let us reason together... though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.'

title: What will the nations beat their swords into?
answer: Plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks.

title: What sign was given to Ahaz?
answer: 'A virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.'
note: Matthew 1:23 reads the Greek 'parthenos' of the Septuagint as decisive for the virgin birth.

title: What does Isaiah say about those who wait upon the LORD?
answer: They renew their strength, mount up with wings as eagles, run and not be weary.

title: What does God say about his glory and graven images?
answer: 'My glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images.'

title: What does Isaiah 55 say about God's thoughts and ways?
answer: They are higher than ours as the heavens are higher than the earth.

title: What does Isaiah say God's word will not do?
answer: It shall not return unto him void, but shall accomplish that which he pleases.

title: Which Isaiah passage did Jesus read at Nazareth?
answer: 'The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me... to preach good tidings unto the meek.'
note: Jesus stopped mid-verse, before 'the day of vengeance,' marking the present age as the acceptable year.

title: How does Isaiah describe our righteousnesses?
answer: 'All our righteousnesses are as filthy rags.'

title: What two evils did Judah commit, per Jeremiah?
answer: They forsook the fountain of living waters and hewed out broken cisterns.

title: What does Jeremiah say about the human heart?
answer: 'The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?'

title: What did God promise in Jeremiah 29:11-13?
answer: Thoughts of peace and an expected end, and that seeking him with the whole heart would find him.

title: What name is given to the righteous Branch?
answer: 'THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS' (Jehovah Tsidkenu).

title: Who rescued Jeremiah from the miry dungeon?
answer: Ebed-melech the Ethiopian.

title: What is new every morning, per Lamentations?
answer: The LORD's mercies — 'great is thy faithfulness.'

title: What did Ezekiel eat, and how did it taste?
answer: A roll of a book; it was in his mouth as honey for sweetness.

title: What departed from the temple in Ezekiel's vision?
answer: The glory of the LORD, moving by stages from the threshold to the mountain east of the city.

title: What proverb about sour grapes did God forbid?
answer: That the children's teeth are set on edge — 'the soul that sinneth, it shall die.'

title: Who are rebuked as shepherds feeding themselves?
answer: The shepherds of Israel, replaced by God himself as shepherd.
note: Jesus' 'I am the good shepherd' (John 10:11) is a direct claim on this passage — and thus on deity.

title: What is the closing name of the city in Ezekiel?
answer: 'THE LORD IS THERE' (Jehovah Shammah).

title: What were the Hebrew names of Daniel's three friends?
answer: Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah — renamed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.

title: What was the three friends' answer about deliverance?
answer: 'Our God is able to deliver us... but if not, we will not serve thy gods.'

title: What humbled Nebuchadnezzar for seven times?
answer: He was driven from men to eat grass as oxen until he acknowledged heaven rules.

title: What is the prophecy of the seventy weeks about?
answer: Seventy sevens decreed to finish transgression, make reconciliation, and bring in everlasting righteousness.

title: Whom did Hosea marry, and at what cost did he redeem her?
answer: Gomer; he bought her for fifteen pieces of silver and an homer and a half of barley.

title: What do Hosea's children's names mean?
answer: Jezreel ('God scatters'), Lo-ruhamah ('not pitied'), Lo-ammi ('not my people').
note: Paul cites the reversal of these names in Rom 9:25-26 as warrant for the calling of the Gentiles.

title: What does Joel call locust years?
answer: 'The years that the locust hath eaten,' which God promises to restore.

title: What plumbline vision did Amos see?
answer: A plumbline set in the midst of Israel, measuring the nation for judgment.

title: What famine did Amos foretell?
answer: 'Not a famine of bread... but of hearing the words of the LORD.'

title: How long was Jonah in the fish, and what did Jesus make of it?
answer: Three days and three nights — the sign of Jonah, pointing to his own burial and rising.

title: What plant sheltered Jonah, and what did God teach by it?
answer: A gourd; God taught Jonah to pity Nineveh's 120,000 as Jonah pitied the plant.

title: What question does Habakkuk open with?
answer: 'O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!'

title: What does Zephaniah say the LORD does over his people?
answer: 'He will joy over thee with singing.'

title: What did Haggai say the latter house's glory would be?
answer: Greater than the former, and in that place God would give peace.

title: What did Zechariah see in the vision of Joshua the high priest?
answer: Joshua in filthy garments, accused by Satan, then clothed with change of raiment.
note: A picture of imputed righteousness: the accusation is not answered by Joshua's merit but by God's rebuke and re-clothing.

title: Whom shall they look upon, per Zechariah 12?
answer: 'Me whom they have pierced,' and mourn as for an only son.

title: What does Malachi say God hates?
answer: Putting away — treacherous divorce against the wife of one's covenant.

title: What test does Malachi permit concerning tithes?
answer: 'Prove me now herewith... if I will not open you the windows of heaven.'

title: What book of remembrance is mentioned in Malachi?
answer: One written before God for them that feared the LORD and thought upon his name.

title: What image does Malachi give the coming Sun of righteousness?
answer: He arises 'with healing in his wings.'

title: What is a prophet's primary function in Israel?
answer: To be a covenant prosecutor, calling Israel back to the Law, not chiefly to predict.
note: Prediction serves prosecution: the future is announced as the covenant's stated consequence, which is why the prophets quote Deuteronomy constantly.

title: What test did Israel have for a true prophet?
answer: That his word came to pass and that he did not call people to other gods.
note: Both tests are needed: accuracy alone is insufficient if the message leads away from the LORD.

title: What is the 'day of the LORD'?
answer: A coming day of divine intervention, judgment first on the nations and then on Israel herself.
note: Amos shocks his hearers by inverting their expectation: the day they longed for is darkness and not light, because judgment begins at God's house.

title: What is the remnant theme?
answer: That God preserves a faithful minority through judgment.
note: Isaiah names his son Shear-jashub, 'a remnant shall return' — the doctrine is walked around Jerusalem in the form of a child.

title: How does Isaiah describe idolatry's absurdity?
answer: A man burns half a log for warmth and worships the other half as a god.
note: Isaiah 40-48 argues monotheism polemically: only the LORD declares the end from the beginning, which is the test he sets for rival gods.

title: What claim does God make in Isaiah 45:5?
answer: 'I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me.'
note: Verse 23's 'unto me every knee shall bow' is applied directly to Christ in Phil 2:10 — an unmistakable identification of Jesus with YHWH.

title: Who is Cyrus called in Isaiah?
answer: God's anointed — 'his messiah' — though a pagan king who did not know him.
note: The only non-Israelite called messiah in Scripture, demonstrating that God's sovereignty extends over rulers who never acknowledge him.

title: What does Isaiah 53 say about the Servant's silence?
answer: He opened not his mouth, as a lamb brought to the slaughter.
note: Quoted by the Ethiopian eunuch in Acts 8:32, whose question 'of whom speaketh the prophet?' occasions the first recorded Gentile conversion.

title: What was Jeremiah's temple sermon?
answer: A warning not to trust the lying words 'the temple of the LORD' as a guarantee of safety.
note: He points to Shiloh, already destroyed, as proof that God will abandon a sanctuary that shelters injustice — and is nearly executed for it (Jer 26).

title: What did Jeremiah advise the exiles to do in Babylon?
answer: Build houses, plant gardens, marry, and seek the peace of the city.
note: The most striking political counsel in the Old Testament: pray for the welfare of the empire that destroyed you, because your welfare is bound up in it.

title: How does the New Covenant differ from the old, per Jeremiah?
answer: The law will be written on hearts, all shall know the LORD, and sin will be remembered no more.
note: The longest Old Testament passage quoted in the New (Heb 8:8-12), and the source of the term 'New Testament' itself.

title: What did Jeremiah do to enact hope during the siege?
answer: He bought a field at Anathoth, sealing the deed as a sign of return.
note: A property investment as prophecy: 'houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land.'

title: What does Ezekiel's watchman commission require?
answer: That he warn the wicked, or their blood be required at his hand.
note: Paul echoes it at Ephesus: 'I am pure from the blood of all men' (Acts 20:26) — faithful warning discharges the messenger's responsibility.

title: What signs did Ezekiel perform with his own body?
answer: Lying on his side for hundreds of days, eating measured rations, and shaving his head and beard.
note: The prophet's body becomes the message. Ezekiel's mute period and his wife's death enacted as a sign are the tradition's extreme cases.

title: What restoration does Ezekiel 36 promise?
answer: A new heart and a new spirit, with God's Spirit put within to cause obedience.
note: This is the passage Jesus expects Nicodemus, 'a master of Israel,' to recognise behind the demand to be born of water and Spirit (John 3:10).

title: What is the meaning of Daniel's four kingdoms?
answer: A succession of empires, ended by a kingdom set up by God that shall never be destroyed.
note: Interpreters divide over whether the fourth is Greece or Rome, but all agree the point is that human empire is temporary and God's is not.

title: What is significant about Daniel's prayer of confession?
answer: He confesses 'we have sinned' though he is among the most blameless figures in Scripture.
note: Solidarity in confession — Daniel prays as a member of a guilty people rather than as an exception to them, as Nehemiah and Ezra also do.

title: What did Gabriel tell Daniel about his prayer?
answer: That at the beginning of his supplications the commandment came forth.
note: Daniel 10:12-13 adds that the answer was delayed twenty-one days by the prince of Persia — a rare glimpse of unseen conflict behind delayed prayer.

title: What does Hosea reveal about God's inner life?
answer: 'How shall I give thee up, Ephraim?... mine heart is turned within me.'
note: The boldest anthropopathic language in the prophets: divine judgment is portrayed as costly to God himself, not detached.

title: What is Joel's promise about the Spirit?
answer: That God will pour out his Spirit upon all flesh — sons, daughters, old, young, servants.
note: Peter's Pentecost sermon claims this is fulfilled, and the explicit inclusion of daughters and servants is the charter text for the movement's breadth.

title: What is Amos' most famous demand?
answer: 'Let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.'
note: Spoken against festivals and solemn assemblies God says he hates — worship divorced from justice is treated as an offence, not a partial credit.

title: What is Micah's contrast between sacrifice and obedience?
answer: Thousands of rams and rivers of oil are refused; justice, mercy and humility are required.
note: Not an abolition of sacrifice but a ranking, consistent with 1 Sam 15:22 and Hos 6:6 — the cult never substitutes for the character it presupposes.

title: How does Habakkuk's argument progress?
answer: From complaint about Judah's sin, to horror at Babylon as the remedy, to worship in the dark.
note: The book models honest wrestling ending not in answers but in trust: 'yet I will rejoice in the LORD.'

title: What does Zechariah's night vision of the lampstand teach?
answer: 'Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.'
