answer: One like unto the Son of man amid seven golden candlesticks, holding seven stars in his right hand.

title: What are the seven stars and seven candlesticks?
answer: The angels of the seven churches, and the seven churches themselves.

title: What promise is given to Smyrna?
answer: 'Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.'

title: What does Christ say at the door in Revelation 3?
answer: 'Behold, I stand at the door, and knock.'

title: What is around the throne in Revelation 4?
answer: A rainbow like an emerald, twenty-four elders, and four beasts full of eyes.

title: What do the four living creatures say continually?
answer: 'Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come.'

title: How is the Lamb described when John looks for the Lion?
answer: 'A Lamb as it had been slain,' with seven horns and seven eyes.
note: John hears 'Lion' and sees 'Lamb' — Revelation's central reinterpretation of what conquest means.

title: What are the four horsemen and their colours?
answer: White, red, black and pale — conquest, war, famine and death.

title: What is under the fifth seal?
answer: The souls of the martyrs, crying 'How long, O Lord?' and given white robes.

title: What is the name of the star that falls in Revelation 8?
answer: Wormwood, which makes a third of the waters bitter.

title: What did the little book taste like to John?
answer: Sweet as honey in his mouth, but bitter in his belly.

title: How long do the two witnesses prophesy?
answer: A thousand two hundred and threescore days, clothed in sackcloth.

title: What happens at the seventh trumpet?
answer: Voices declare, 'The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ.'

title: Who is the woman clothed with the sun?
answer: A figure variously read as Israel, the Church, or Mary, bearing the man child.

title: What is the number of the beast?
answer: Six hundred threescore and six — 'the number of a man.'

title: What do the three angels of Revelation 14 proclaim?
answer: The everlasting gospel, the fall of Babylon, and warning against the beast's mark.

title: What song do the victors sing by the sea of glass?
answer: 'The song of Moses... and the song of the Lamb.'

title: How long is Satan bound in Revelation 20?
answer: A thousand years, then loosed a little season.
note: Premillennial, amillennial and postmillennial readings all turn on whether this thousand years is future, present, or symbolic.

title: What books are opened at the judgment?
answer: The books of works, and 'another book... which is the book of life.'

title: What is the second death?
answer: The lake of fire, into which death and hell are cast.

title: How is the New Jerusalem described coming down?
answer: 'Prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.'

title: What will God do with every tear?
answer: 'God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes.'

title: What grows on either side of the river of life?
answer: The tree of life, whose leaves are for the healing of the nations.
note: Scripture ends where it began — a tree of life — but now open, not guarded by cherubim.

title: What warning closes Revelation about the book's words?
answer: Against adding to or taking from the words of the prophecy.

title: What are the four main schools of interpreting Revelation?
answer: Preterist, historicist, futurist and idealist.
note: Preterist reads it as first-century, historicist as church history, futurist as end-times, idealist as timeless symbol; most readers blend them.

title: What Old Testament book most shapes Revelation's imagery?
answer: Ezekiel, with Daniel, Isaiah, Zechariah and Exodus close behind.
note: Revelation contains no formal quotations but hundreds of allusions — it is written for readers already saturated in Hebrew Scripture.

title: Why is the number seven so prominent?
answer: It signifies completeness — seven churches, seals, trumpets, bowls, spirits, stars.
note: Numbers in apocalyptic are qualitative: seven means whole, twelve means the people of God, and 666 falls short of seven three times over.

title: What does Revelation say about its own reading?
answer: Blessed is he that readeth and they that hear the words of this prophecy.
note: The blessing presupposes public oral reading to a congregation — Revelation was designed to be heard aloud in one sitting.

title: What is promised to the overcomer in each of the seven letters?
answer: A distinct reward — the tree of life, the crown, hidden manna, the morning star, white raiment, a pillar, and the throne.
note: Each promise answers that city's particular pressure; the reward is tailored to the temptation.

title: What is significant about Laodicea's lukewarmness?
answer: The city's water arrived tepid via aqueduct, neither hot for healing nor cold for refreshment.
note: The image is local and precise: the problem is uselessness, not moderate enthusiasm.

title: Who are the twenty-four elders?
answer: Likely the twelve patriarchs with the twelve apostles, representing the whole people of God.
note: They cast their crowns before the throne — every reward received is returned to the giver.

title: What is the scroll with seven seals?
answer: The book of God's purposes for history, which none but the Lamb can open.
note: John weeps at the prospect of history having no meaning; the resolution is not information but a person worthy to unfold it.

title: What new song is sung to the Lamb?
answer: That he was slain and redeemed men out of every kindred, tongue, people and nation.
note: The fourfold formula recurs seven times in Revelation, insisting the redeemed community is irreducibly multi-ethnic.

title: What do the martyrs under the altar ask?
answer: 'How long, O Lord... dost thou not judge and avenge our blood?'
note: The imprecatory psalms reappear in heaven itself, showing that the cry for justice is not sub-Christian but eschatological.

title: What is the sealing of the servants of God for?
answer: Protection and ownership before the judgments proceed.
note: It parallels the Passover blood and Ezekiel 9's mark — the seal does not exempt from suffering but marks belonging through it.

title: Where does the great multitude come from?
answer: Out of great tribulation, having washed their robes white in the blood of the Lamb.
note: The paradox of whitening by blood is Revelation's compressed doctrine of atonement.

title: What do the prayers of the saints do in Revelation 8?
answer: They ascend with incense before God, and fire from the altar is cast to the earth.
note: Prayer is depicted as causally connected to history's judgments — one of Scripture's strongest images of intercession's weight.

title: What is the significance of the two witnesses' resurrection?
answer: After three and a half days they stand and ascend, and their enemies see it.
note: Their career mirrors Christ's — testimony, death in the city, resurrection, ascension — modelling the church's own pattern.

title: What is the war in heaven about?
answer: Michael and his angels cast out the dragon, the accuser of the brethren.
note: Verse 11 gives the means of victory as the blood of the Lamb, the word of testimony, and not loving their lives to the death.

title: What does the dragon do after being cast down?
answer: He persecutes the woman and makes war with the remnant of her seed.
note: Persecution is presented as evidence of the enemy's defeat and short time, not of his strength.

title: What is the mark of the beast contrasted with?
answer: The seal of God on the foreheads of his servants.
note: Both marks are on the forehead or hand — allegiance is visible and total; no one is unmarked in Revelation's world.

title: What is said of those who die in the Lord?
answer: 'Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord... their works do follow them.'
note: One of only seven beatitudes in Revelation, and the one most often read at Christian funerals.

title: What does the harvest imagery of Revelation 14 depict?
answer: Two reapings — a grain harvest and a grape harvest trodden in the winepress.
note: Read by many as the gathering of the redeemed and the judgment of the wicked in parallel.

title: How is Babylon's fall announced and lamented?
answer: By an angel's cry, and mourned by kings, merchants and shipmasters who profited from her.
note: The lament is an economic one — chapter 18 is a devastating critique of an empire built on trade, ending with 'the souls of men' as cargo (18:13).

title: What are the names of the returning Christ in Revelation 19?
answer: Faithful and True, The Word of God, and KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS.
note: His robe is dipped in blood before the battle begins — the victory is won by his own death, not by the coming conflict.

title: What is the testimony of Jesus said to be?
answer: The spirit of prophecy.
note: Said by an angel refusing worship — twice in Revelation John tries to worship an angel and is stopped (19:10; 22:8-9).

title: What are the dimensions and shape of the New Jerusalem?
answer: A cube, twelve thousand furlongs in length, breadth and height.
note: The only other cube in Scripture is the Holy of Holies (1 Kgs 6:20) — the whole city is the sanctuary, so no temple is needed (21:22).

title: What is absent from the New Jerusalem that was central to the old?
answer: A temple, for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it.
note: The trajectory of Scripture ends with mediating structures removed, since the barrier they mediated is gone.

title: How does Revelation invite the reader at the close?
answer: 'Let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.'
note: The Bible's last invitation is universal and free — the Spirit and the bride issue it jointly, making evangelism the church's final act.

title: What is the last prayer of the Bible?
answer: 'Even so, come, Lord Jesus.'
note: It renders the Aramaic 'Maranatha' of 1 Cor 16:22, one of the oldest surviving Christian prayers.

title: Which books appear in the Revised Version's Apocrypha section?
answer: 1-2 Esdras, Tobit, Judith, additions to Esther, Wisdom, Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), Baruch, Letter of Jeremiah, Song of the Three, Susanna, Bel and the Dragon, Prayer of Manasses, and 1-2 Maccabees.

title: What does the Greek word "apocrypha" literally mean?
answer: "Hidden away" — used by Jerome to mark books outside the Hebrew canon.

title: What does "deuterocanonical" mean, and who coined it?
answer: "Second canon" — coined in 1566 by Sixtus of Siena, over a millennium after "Apocrypha."

title: What is the story of Tobit about?
answer: A blinded righteous Israelite in exile, his son Tobias, the angel Raphael in disguise, and Sarah delivered from a demon.

title: What does Judith recount?
answer: A widow who saves her city by beheading the Assyrian general Holofernes.

title: What is the Wisdom of Solomon known for?
answer: Its portrait of immortality of the righteous and its personification of Wisdom.
note: Its language about the "effulgence of eternal light" echoes in Hebrews 1:3.

title: What kind of book is Sirach (Ecclesiasticus)?
answer: A long collection of practical wisdom by Jesus ben Sira, with a famous "praise of famous men" section.

title: Who was Susanna, and how was she vindicated?
answer: A virtuous wife falsely accused by two elders, cleared when young Daniel cross-examined them separately.

title: What does Bel and the Dragon demonstrate?
answer: Daniel exposing idol-priests' fraud and destroying a dragon — polemic against idolatry.

title: What is the Prayer of Manasses?
answer: A penitential prayer attributed to the repentant king Manasseh of Judah.

title: What historical events does 1 Maccabees record?
answer: The Maccabean revolt against Antiochus IV Epiphanes and the rededication of the temple.
note: That rededication is the origin of Hanukkah, mentioned as the "feast of the dedication" in John 10:22.

title: Which Apocryphal passage is cited in the purgatory debate?
answer: 2 Maccabees 12:43-46, where offerings are made for the dead.

title: What is the Song of the Three Children?
answer: A hymn of praise placed in the mouths of Daniel's companions inside the fiery furnace.

title: What does Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles say about these books?
answer: They may be read "for example of life and instruction of manners," but not used to establish doctrine.

title: How many books did the Revised Version issue in its Apocrypha volume?
answer: Fourteen titles in the traditional English arrangement, published separately in 1895.

title: What are 1 and 2 Esdras in the English Apocrypha?
answer: Two books distinct from canonical Ezra–Nehemiah; 1 Esdras retells Josiah to Ezra, 2 Esdras is apocalyptic.

title: What famous question contest appears in 1 Esdras?
answer: Three guardsmen debate what is strongest; Zerubbabel answers 'truth,' and truth prevails.
note: 'Great is truth, and mighty above all things' passed into common European proverb.

title: What are the Additions to Esther?
answer: Six Greek passages supplying prayers and explicit mention of God, absent from the Hebrew text.

title: What does Wisdom of Solomon say about death's origin?
answer: 'God made not death'; through envy of the devil came death into the world.

title: What famous verse of Wisdom concerns the souls of the righteous?
answer: 'The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and there shall no torment touch them.'

title: Who was the author of Sirach, and who translated it?
answer: Jesus ben Sira; his grandson translated it into Greek and wrote the prologue.

title: Which Sirach passage is widely read at funerals and memorials?
answer: 'Let us now praise famous men, and our fathers that begat us.'

title: What does Baruch contain?
answer: A confession of exile, a wisdom poem, and a consolation to Jerusalem, attributed to Jeremiah's scribe.

title: Who is the villain of Judith, and how does she prevail?
answer: Holofernes, Nebuchadnezzar's general, whom Judith beheads after gaining his trust.

title: What archangel is named in Tobit?
answer: Raphael, who travels with Tobias disguised as a kinsman.

title: What does Tobit teach about almsgiving?
answer: 'Alms doth deliver from death, and shall purge away all sin.'
note: This verse is central to disputes over merit; Reformers rejected it as a basis for doctrine precisely because they rejected the book's canonicity.

title: What festival does 1 Maccabees explain the origin of?
answer: The rededication of the temple, kept as Hanukkah — the feast of dedication of John 10:22.

title: Who were the Maccabean brothers' father and chief leader?
answer: Mattathias the priest; his son Judas 'Maccabeus' led the revolt.

title: What martyrdom story is told in 2 Maccabees?
answer: A mother and her seven sons tortured under Antiochus, confessing resurrection hope.
note: Hebrews 11:35 — 'that they might obtain a better resurrection' — appears to allude to this account.

title: What creation statement appears in 2 Maccabees 7:28?
answer: That God made heaven and earth 'not of things that were' — an early creatio ex nihilo formula.

title: How did the Reformers and Rome differ on these books at Trent?
answer: Trent (1546) affirmed them as canonical; the Reformers kept them as edifying but not doctrinally binding.

title: Where did the King James Version originally print the Apocrypha?
answer: Between the Testaments, as a separate section — the 1611 edition included it.

title: What is 3 and 4 Maccabees' status in English Bibles?
answer: Absent from the RV Apocrypha; they appear in Orthodox canons and appendices.

title: Why did the Revised Version include the Apocrypha at all?
answer: Because the KJV of 1611 had included it, and the revisers were commissioned to revise the whole.
note: The Apocrypha volume appeared ten years after the Old Testament, produced by a smaller company of scholars.

title: What is the difference between 'apocrypha' and 'pseudepigrapha'?
answer: Apocrypha are the disputed books in some canons; pseudepigrapha are works falsely attributed to ancient figures.
note: 1 Enoch and Jubilees are pseudepigrapha in Western reckoning, though 1 Enoch is canonical in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.

title: Which New Testament book appears to quote 1 Enoch?
answer: Jude, citing Enoch's prophecy of the Lord coming with ten thousands of his saints.
note: Citation is not canonisation — Paul also quotes Greek poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12) without granting them scriptural status.

title: What language was Sirach originally written in?
answer: Hebrew; Hebrew fragments were later found at Masada and in the Cairo Geniza.
note: The grandson's prologue is the earliest external witness to the threefold division of the Hebrew Bible — law, prophets and other writings.

title: What does Wisdom of Solomon say about the righteous man's persecution?
answer: That the ungodly test him with shame and torture to see if God will defend him.
note: The passage's language closely parallels the mockery at the cross in Matt 27:43, and early Christians read it as prophetic.

title: What is Susanna's place in the book of Daniel?
answer: An addition placed as chapter 13 in the Greek and Latin traditions.
note: Daniel cross-examines the elders separately about the tree they claim to have seen — often cited as the earliest recorded courtroom cross-examination.

title: How did Daniel expose the priests of Bel?
answer: By scattering ashes on the temple floor to reveal the footprints of the priests who ate the offerings by night.
note: The story belongs to a broader Jewish tradition of anti-idol satire also found in Isaiah 44 and the Epistle of Jeremy.

title: What is 2 Esdras notable for?
answer: Its seven visions wrestling with theodicy after Jerusalem's destruction.
note: Chapter 14 tells of Ezra dictating ninety-four books, twenty-four public and seventy secret — an early reflection on canon formation.

title: How does Tobit end?
answer: With Tobit's sight restored, Tobias married, and a hymn of praise for Jerusalem.
note: The book's marriage prayer — that they may grow old together — is still used in some Christian wedding liturgies.

title: What is the theological argument of 2 Maccabees 12 regarding the dead?
answer: That Judas made atonement for the fallen, that they might be delivered from sin.
note: The single clearest scriptural basis Rome cites for prayers for the dead; the Reformers' rejection of it followed directly from rejecting the book's canonicity.

title: What is the Prayer of Azariah?
answer: A prayer of confession spoken in the fiery furnace, inserted into Daniel 3 in the Greek.
note: It laments that Israel has no prince, prophet, or place to offer sacrifice — offering instead 'a contrite heart and humble spirit.'

title: What is the Benedicite, and where does it come from?
answer: The canticle 'O all ye works of the Lord, bless ye the Lord,' from the Song of the Three Children.
note: Retained in the Book of Common Prayer as a canticle at Morning Prayer, so Anglicans sing apocryphal text liturgically while classing it as non-canonical.

title: What historical value does 1 Maccabees have?
answer: It is a sober, largely reliable account of the Jewish revolt from 175 to 134 BC.
note: Unlike 2 Maccabees it contains few miracles and no explicit doctrine of resurrection, and scholars generally rate it the better history.

title: Who is the villain of the Maccabean books?
answer: Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who desecrated the temple with a pagan altar.
note: His desecration is widely regarded as the 'abomination of desolation' of Daniel 11:31, to which Jesus refers in Matt 24:15.

title: How did Jerome regard these books?
answer: As edifying for the church but not for establishing doctrine — he coined the term 'apocrypha' for them.
note: Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles reproduces Jerome's judgment almost verbatim, which is why the Anglican position is often called Hieronymian.

title: How many books are in the Protestant Bible, and how are they divided?
answer: 66 — 39 Old Testament and 27 New Testament.
note: 39 and 27 is a Christian arrangement; the same Old Testament material is counted as 24 books in the Hebrew Bible, which groups the minor prophets as one and joins Samuel, Kings and Chronicles.

title: In what languages was the Bible originally written?
answer: Hebrew (most of the Old Testament), Aramaic (parts of Daniel and Ezra), and Koine Greek (the New Testament).
note: Hebrew, Aramaic (Dan 2-7, Ezra 4-7, a verse of Jeremiah) and Koine Greek — the common trade language rather than a sacred dialect, which is itself theologically significant.

title: What is the Septuagint?
answer: The Greek translation of the Old Testament made from the 3rd century BC, widely used by the early Church.
note: Its readings often differ from the Masoretic Text, and where the New Testament quotes the Old it usually follows the Greek — Hebrews 10:5's 'a body hast thou prepared me' is a well-known instance.

title: What is a covenant, and how many major ones does Scripture trace?
answer: A binding relationship established by God; commonly counted as Noahic, Abrahamic, Mosaic, Davidic, and New.

title: What is typology?
answer: Reading persons, events or institutions of the Old Testament as divinely intended patterns fulfilled in Christ.
note: Typology differs from allegory in requiring a real historical correspondence rather than a coded meaning; the New Testament signals it with words like 'figure' (Rom 5:14) and 'shadow' (Col 2:17).

title: What is the difference between justification and sanctification?
answer: Justification is God's declaration that the believer is righteous; sanctification is the ongoing work of being made holy.
note: Justification is instantaneous, declarative and equal in all believers; sanctification is progressive, transformative and unequal — confusing them produces either legalism or presumption.

title: What is the difference between propitiation and expiation?
answer: Propitiation turns aside wrath directed at the sinner; expiation removes the guilt of the sin itself. Scripture holds both.

title: What is the hypostatic union?
answer: The doctrine that Christ is one Person in two natures, fully God and fully man, without confusion or division.
note: Defined at the Council of Chalcedon in 451.

title: What are the traditional attributes of God grouped as?
answer: Incommunicable (eternity, immutability, omnipresence, omnipotence, omniscience) and communicable (holiness, justice, love, mercy, faithfulness).

title: What is general revelation versus special revelation?
answer: General: God made known through creation and conscience. Special: God made known through Scripture and supremely in Christ.

title: What is the canon, and what criteria shaped its recognition?
answer: The list of books recognised as Scripture; recognised by apostolic origin, orthodoxy of content, and widespread use in the churches.
note: Apostolicity, orthodoxy, catholicity and liturgical use functioned as criteria of recognition rather than as tests conferring authority — the church discerned the canon, it did not create it.

title: What are the first four Ecumenical Councils and their chief decisions?
answer: Nicaea 325 (the Son is of one substance with the Father), Constantinople 381 (the deity of the Spirit), Ephesus 431 (Mary as Theotokos, Christ's unity of Person), Chalcedon 451 (two natures in one Person).

title: What are the traditional marks of the Church in the Creed?
answer: One, holy, catholic (universal) and apostolic.

title: What are the ordinances or sacraments recognised across traditions?
answer: All hold baptism and the Lord's Supper; Catholic and Orthodox recognise seven, adding confirmation/chrismation, penance, anointing, orders, and marriage.

title: What does "eschatology" mean, and what four events does it centre on?
answer: The doctrine of last things — Christ's return, the resurrection, the final judgment, and the eternal state.

title: What is the Trinity, stated in one sentence?
answer: One God in three co-equal, co-eternal Persons — Father, Son and Holy Spirit — one in essence, distinct in relation.

title: What is the difference between the immanent and economic Trinity?
answer: The immanent Trinity is God in himself; the economic Trinity is God as revealed in creation and redemption.

title: What is meant by 'original sin'?
answer: The corrupt condition inherited from Adam, distinguished from actual sins committed.
note: Traditions differ on whether it destroys the will (Augustinian/Reformed) or wounds it (Catholic/Orthodox).

title: What is prevenient grace?
answer: Grace that precedes and enables a human response to God, prominent in Wesleyan and Catholic theology.

title: What is regeneration?
answer: The new birth — the Spirit's act of imparting spiritual life to the dead sinner.

title: What is imputation?
answer: The reckoning of Christ's righteousness to the believer and the believer's sin to Christ.

title: What is the difference between mortal and venial sin?
answer: A Catholic distinction between sin that destroys charity in the soul and sin that wounds without destroying it.

title: What are the theological and cardinal virtues?
answer: Theological: faith, hope, charity. Cardinal: prudence, justice, temperance, fortitude.

title: What is the analogy of faith?
answer: The principle that Scripture interprets Scripture, obscure passages read by clear ones.

title: What are the four classic senses of Scripture?
answer: Literal, allegorical, moral (tropological), and anagogical.

title: What is inerrancy versus infallibility?
answer: Inerrancy: Scripture is without error in all it affirms. Infallibility: it cannot fail in its purpose of salvation.

title: What is apostolic succession?
answer: The doctrine that bishops stand in an unbroken line of ordination from the apostles.

title: What is the difference between transubstantiation, consubstantiation, real spiritual presence, and memorialism?
answer: Four Eucharistic views: substance changed; Christ 'in, with, under'; true spiritual feeding by faith; remembrance only.
note: All four claim John 6 and 1 Corinthians 11; the divide is metaphysical as much as exegetical.

title: What is the communion of saints?
answer: The fellowship of all believers, living and departed, in Christ.

title: What is the difference between latria, dulia and hyperdulia?
answer: Worship due to God alone; honour given to saints; the higher honour given to Mary in Catholic usage.

title: What is theosis or deification?
answer: The Eastern doctrine that believers participate in the divine energies, becoming by grace what God is by nature.

title: What is the filioque, and why did it divide East and West?
answer: The Western addition that the Spirit proceeds 'and from the Son'; the East objected to both the doctrine and the unilateral change.

title: What are the five solas of the Reformation?
answer: Scripture alone, faith alone, grace alone, Christ alone, glory to God alone.

title: What are the traditional means of grace?
answer: Word, sacrament and prayer, through which God ordinarily conveys grace.

title: What is the difference between amillennialism, premillennialism and postmillennialism?
answer: Christ returns after a symbolic reign; before a literal thousand years; after a gospel-triumphant age.

title: What is the intermediate state?
answer: The condition of the soul between death and resurrection, variously described as sleep, paradise, or conscious rest.

title: What is meant by 'the perspicuity of Scripture'?
answer: That Scripture's saving message is clear enough for ordinary readers, though not all passages are equally plain.

title: What is natural law?
answer: Moral order knowable by reason from creation, distinct from but consistent with revealed law.

title: What is the difference between common and saving grace?
answer: Common grace restrains evil and gives good to all; saving grace effects redemption.

title: What are the classic marks of a true church at the Reformation?
answer: The word rightly preached, the sacraments rightly administered, and discipline rightly exercised.

title: What is the difference between exegesis and eisegesis?
answer: Drawing meaning out of the text versus reading meaning into it.
note: The practical test is whether a reading would be recognised by the original author and audience.

title: What is progressive revelation?
answer: The principle that God disclosed truth gradually, culminating in Christ.
note: It explains earlier accommodations without calling them errors, and forbids reading later doctrine back as though it were always explicit.

title: What is the difference between the ordo salutis and the historia salutis?
answer: The order of salvation in an individual versus the history of salvation across the ages.
note: Confusing the two produces most of the classic misunderstandings between Reformed and dispensational readings.

title: What is meant by the 'already and not yet'?
answer: That the kingdom has genuinely arrived in Christ but is not yet consummated.
note: This inaugurated eschatology resolves much apparent tension: believers are truly redeemed and still await 'the redemption of our body.'

title: What is union with Christ?
answer: The believer's incorporation into Christ, the source of every other saving benefit.
note: Calvin called it the doctrine on which all others hang: justification and sanctification are distinct gifts received in the one Christ, so neither can be had without the other.

title: What is the difference between monergism and synergism?
answer: Whether regeneration is God's work alone or a cooperation of divine and human wills.
note: The debate is chiefly about the first moment of new life; nearly all traditions affirm cooperation in sanctification thereafter.

title: What is the covenant of works and the covenant of grace?
answer: A Reformed framework contrasting Adam's probation with the gracious covenant in Christ.
note: Lutherans and Catholics generally decline the schema while affirming the underlying Adam–Christ contrast Paul draws.

title: What is meant by the perspicuity and the sufficiency of Scripture?
answer: That its saving message is clear and that it contains all things necessary for salvation.
note: Neither claims every passage is easy — 2 Peter 3:16 concedes some things are hard to understand.

title: What is the regulative versus the normative principle of worship?
answer: Worship may include only what Scripture commands, versus whatever it does not forbid.
note: The difference explains why some traditions sing only psalms without instruments while others use whatever aids devotion.

title: What are the classical arguments for God's existence?
answer: Cosmological, teleological, ontological, moral and the argument from religious experience.
note: Scripture never argues for God's existence, so these are theological reflections on general revelation, not biblical proofs.

title: What is theodicy?
answer: The attempt to justify God's goodness and power in the face of evil.
note: The term was coined by Leibniz in 1710; the Bible's own approach in Job is to decline the project and present God instead.

title: What is the difference between an attribute and a person of God?
answer: Attributes are what God is; Persons are who God is, distinguished by eternal relations.
note: Confusing the two produces modalism, in which the Persons become mere aspects rather than genuine relations.

title: What is divine simplicity?
answer: That God is not composed of parts; his attributes are identical with his essence.
note: Classical theism holds God does not have love but is love; some modern theologians contest the doctrine as over-philosophical.

title: What is divine impassibility, and why is it debated?
answer: That God is not subject to involuntary emotional change; critics argue it undercuts a suffering God.
note: Defenders distinguish passion (being acted upon) from genuine love and compassion, which they affirm without qualification.

title: What is the difference between the visible and invisible church?
answer: The institution as it appears, and the total company of the truly regenerate known to God.
note: The parable of the wheat and tares grounds the distinction, and explains why the church contains hypocrites without ceasing to be the church.

title: What are the classical spiritual disciplines?
answer: Prayer, fasting, study, worship, service, solitude, silence, confession and celebration.
note: Jesus teaches giving, praying and fasting with the same 'when you' formula — assuming all three as ordinary Christian practice.

title: What is the difference between imputed and infused righteousness?
answer: Righteousness credited to the believer's account, versus righteousness poured into and transforming them.
note: This single distinction is arguably the deepest divide of the Reformation, more fundamental than indulgences or papal authority.

title: What is the sensus plenior?
answer: A fuller sense of a text intended by God beyond what the human author consciously knew.
note: Peter says the prophets searched their own writings to learn what they meant — Scripture itself suggests authors could write more than they grasped.

title: What is meant by the incommunicable attributes of God?
answer: Those not shared with creatures — aseity, infinity, immutability, eternity, omnipresence.
note: The communicable attributes — love, justice, mercy, knowledge — are shared analogically, which is what makes the imago Dei intelligible.

title: What is the difference between apologetics, polemics and catechesis?
answer: Defending the faith to outsiders, contending against error within, and instructing the faithful.
note: Confusing the three is a common pastoral error — catechesis delivered in a polemical register tends to form combatants rather than disciples.

title: What do BC and AD stand for, and who devised AD?
answer: Before Christ and Anno Domini ("in the year of the Lord"); devised by the monk Dionysius Exiguus in 525.

title: Roughly when did the Exodus occur?
answer: Either c. 1446 BC (early date, from 1 Kgs 6:1) or c. 1260 BC (late date) — both defended by serious scholars.

title: When did the united monarchy divide?
answer: About 931 BC, after Solomon's death.

title: When did Assyria destroy the northern kingdom?
answer: 722 BC, when Samaria fell and the ten tribes were deported.

title: When did Jerusalem and the temple fall to Babylon?
answer: 586 BC, under Nebuchadnezzar.

title: What is the "intertestamental" or "silent" period?
answer: Roughly 400 years between Malachi and John the Baptist, spanning Persian, Greek, Maccabean and Roman rule.

title: When did Herod the Great die, and why does it matter for dating Christ's birth?
answer: Most place it in 4 BC; since Matthew sets the nativity before Herod's death, Jesus was likely born c. 6-4 BC.

title: What were the Edict of Milan and the Edict of Thessalonica?
answer: 313 — Constantine legalised Christianity; 380 — Theodosius made Nicene Christianity the empire's official religion.

title: What was the Great Schism, and when?
answer: The 1054 split between the Western (Roman) and Eastern (Orthodox) churches, over papal authority and the filioque among other issues.

title: Why did Pope Gregory XIII delete ten days in October 1582?
answer: To correct the Julian calendar's accumulated drift, restoring the spring equinox to its true date for calculating Easter.
note: England only adopted the Gregorian calendar in 1752, by then needing an eleven-day correction.

title: Roughly when did Abraham live?
answer: About 2000–1800 BC, in the Middle Bronze Age.

title: When did David reign?
answer: Approximately 1010–970 BC.

title: When did the Babylonian exile begin and end?
answer: Deportations from 605 BC, temple destroyed 586 BC, return under Cyrus 538 BC.

title: When was the second temple completed and later expanded?
answer: Completed 516 BC under Zerubbabel; greatly expanded by Herod from 20 BC.

title: When did Alexander the Great conquer the Near East?
answer: 333–331 BC, spreading Greek language that later carried the New Testament.

title: When was the temple destroyed by Rome?
answer: AD 70, under Titus.

title: When were the four Gospels most commonly dated?
answer: Between about AD 60 and 95, with Mark generally earliest and John latest.

title: What did the Council of Nicaea settle, and when?
answer: AD 325 — the Son is homoousios, of one substance with the Father, against Arius.

title: What was the Council of Chalcedon's definition?
answer: AD 451 — one Person in two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation.

title: Who translated the Latin Vulgate, and when?
answer: Jerome, c. AD 382–405.

title: When was the Gutenberg Bible printed?
answer: About 1455, the first major book from movable type in Europe.

title: When did Luther post the Ninety-Five Theses?
answer: 31 October 1517, at Wittenberg.

title: When was the King James Version published, and the Revised Version?
answer: KJV in 1611; the Revised Version New Testament 1881, Old Testament 1885, Apocrypha 1895.

title: What was the Council of Trent, and when?
answer: 1545–1563, the Roman Catholic response to the Reformation, defining canon, justification and sacraments.

title: What were the First and Second Vatican Councils?
answer: Vatican I (1869–70) defined papal infallibility; Vatican II (1962–65) reformed liturgy and ecumenical relations.

title: When were the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered, and why do they matter?
answer: From 1947 at Qumran; they pushed Hebrew manuscript evidence back roughly a thousand years.
note: The Great Isaiah Scroll matched the Masoretic text closely, strongly confirming transmission accuracy.

title: What is the Masoretic Text?
answer: The authoritative Hebrew Old Testament text with vowel points, fixed by the Masoretes c. AD 700–1000.

title: What are Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus?
answer: Fourth-century Greek uncial manuscripts, among the oldest near-complete Bibles, heavily used by the Revised Version.

title: When did the Great Awakening and the modern missionary movement begin?
answer: Awakenings from the 1730s; the modern missionary era from William Carey's departure in 1793.

title: When did the modern Pentecostal movement begin?
answer: Generally dated to Topeka (1901) and the Azusa Street revival (1906–09).

title: What are the major periods of Old Testament history in order?
answer: Patriarchs, Exodus, Conquest, Judges, United Monarchy, Divided Kingdom, Exile, Return.
note: Holding this eight-stage skeleton makes almost every prophetic book locatable, since each prophet speaks into one of the last four stages.

title: When did the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles occur respectively?
answer: Israel to Assyria in 722 BC; Judah to Babylon in stages from 605 to 586 BC.
note: The two exiles are distinct in date, destination and outcome — the northern tribes never returned as a body.

title: Who were the Persian kings relevant to the return?
answer: Cyrus, Darius I, Xerxes (Ahasuerus) and Artaxerxes I.
note: Esther is set under Xerxes, between the temple's completion under Darius and Ezra's mission under Artaxerxes.

title: What happened during the intertestamental period?
answer: Persian, Greek, Ptolemaic, Seleucid and Hasmonean rule, ending with Roman conquest in 63 BC.
note: The synagogue, the Pharisees, the Sadducees and the Septuagint all emerge here — the New Testament world is built in these four centuries.

title: When was the Septuagint translated, and why does it matter?
answer: From the third century BC in Alexandria; it is the Old Testament most New Testament writers quote.
note: Isaiah 7:14's 'parthenos' for the Hebrew 'almah' comes from the LXX, and Matthew's virgin birth citation depends on it.

title: Who were the Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and Zealots?
answer: Legal traditionalists, priestly aristocrats, separatist ascetics, and armed revolutionaries.
note: Sadducees denied resurrection, angels and spirits — Paul exploits precisely this in Acts 23:6 to split the council.

title: When did Jesus most likely die, and how is it dated?
answer: AD 30 or 33, from Pilate's prefecture, Passover timing and Luke's fifteenth year of Tiberius.
note: Both years produce a Friday Passover; the choice usually follows how one harmonises John's chronology with the Synoptics.

title: When were Paul's letters written relative to the Gospels?
answer: Most of Paul's letters predate all four Gospels, from roughly AD 48 to 67.
note: 1 Corinthians 15:3-4, written c. AD 55, contains a creed Paul says he received — pushing the resurrection confession to within a few years of the event.

title: What happened to the apostles, by tradition?
answer: Most died as martyrs; John alone is said to have died of old age in Ephesus.
note: Only two apostolic deaths are recorded in Scripture — James in Acts 12:2 and Judas — the rest come from later church tradition of varying reliability.

title: What were the great persecutions of the early church?
answer: Under Nero, Domitian, Decius, Valerian and finally Diocletian.
note: The Diocletianic persecution from 303 was the most severe and the last, ending within a decade in Constantine's toleration.

title: Who were the Apostolic Fathers?
answer: Clement of Rome, Ignatius, Polycarp, and the writers of the Didache and Barnabas.
note: Their proximity to the apostles makes them a key witness to how the earliest post-apostolic church read the New Testament.

title: What heresies did the early councils address?
answer: Arianism, Apollinarianism, Nestorianism and Eutychianism.
note: Each denied something of Christ's full deity, full humanity, or the unity of his Person — Chalcedon's formula fences off all four at once.

title: What was the Muratorian Fragment?
answer: A late second-century list of New Testament books, the earliest surviving canon list.
note: It already includes the four Gospels, Acts and thirteen Pauline letters, showing the core canon was settled long before any council ruled on it.

title: When did monasticism begin?
answer: With Antony in the Egyptian desert around AD 270 and Pachomius' communities soon after.
note: It arose as persecution ended — when martyrdom ceased to be available, asceticism became the new form of total commitment.

title: What was the Great Schism of 1054 about?
answer: Papal authority and the filioque clause, culminating in mutual excommunications.
note: The 1054 date is symbolic; the real estrangement was centuries of linguistic, political and cultural divergence, sealed by the sack of Constantinople in 1204.

title: Who were the pre-Reformation reformers?
answer: John Wycliffe in England and Jan Hus in Bohemia.
note: Wycliffe's followers produced the first complete English Bible; Hus was burned in 1415 despite a safe conduct, a memory that shaped Luther's caution at Worms.

title: What were the main branches of the Reformation?
answer: Lutheran, Reformed, Anabaptist and Anglican.
note: The Anabaptists were persecuted by Catholics and magisterial Reformers alike, and their insistence on church–state separation later shaped modern religious liberty.

title: What was the Westminster Assembly?
answer: An English assembly (1643-53) producing the Confession and the Larger and Shorter Catechisms.
note: Its Shorter Catechism opens with 'to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever' — arguably the most quoted line in Reformed literature.

title: When did the modern Bible translation movement expand?
answer: From the nineteenth century, accelerating through Bible societies and the twentieth-century missionary movement.
note: The RV of 1881-95 was the first major revision of the KJV and set the pattern of committee revision using older manuscripts.

title: What was the Edinburgh Missionary Conference of 1910?
answer: A landmark gathering usually regarded as the beginning of the modern ecumenical movement.
note: Its watchword, 'the evangelisation of the world in this generation,' eventually led to the World Council of Churches in 1948.
